written. ‒ i voted in favour of the draft legislative resolution of the european parliament on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on safeguard measures provided for in the agreement between the european economic community and the swiss confederation because codification contributes to the clarity and certainty of european union law and stresses the importance of making union law accessible to all citizens and its transparency. i believe that the european union must make it easier and more efficient to find and understand its legal acts, and i believe that the codification is going in that direction.
written. ‒ it is in the european union's interest that all documents are transparent and accessible so that citizens can understand them more easily. for this purpose, european union documents shall be codified where appropriate. the commission proposal for the codification of the agreement between the european economic community and the swiss confederation concerns the amendment of the existing text without affecting the content of the agreement. the agreement between the european economic community and the swiss confederation was signed in 1972 with the aim of developing economic relations by ensuring a level playing field and removing existing obstacles to the establishment of free trade. i support the report by mr andrzej dude, which is based on the opinion of the advisory groups of the legal services of the european parliament, the council and the commission.
written. - council regulation no 2841/72/eec on the safeguard measures provided for in the agreement between the european economic community and the swiss confederation was adopted on 19 december 1972 and has been amended several times. the commission established as early as 1987 the rule that after a dozen amendments to a given act, it must be codified, thus contributing to greater certainty of the correct application of the act. the basic regulation has been amended in so far as it concerns the rules on trade including the implementation of the safeguard clause and the safeguard measures provided for in the agreement. the implementation of the bilateral safeguard clauses in the treaty requires uniform conditions for the adoption of safeguard measures. that implies that those measures should be adopted in accordance with regulation (eu) no 182/2011 of the european parliament and of the council of 16 february 2011 laying down the rules and general principles concerning mechanisms for control by member states of the commission's exercise of implementing powers. the act is of relevance for the regulation of trade between the eu and the swiss confederation. in order to ensure that the proposed codification is correctly applied both between states and between the stakeholders to whom this regulation has legal effect, i consider it necessary as it contributes to greater legal certainty in the application of the act.
written. ‒ since, in the opinion of the consultative working party of the legal services of the european parliament, the council and the commission, the proposal in question is limited to the codification of existing texts without any substantial changes, i support the rapporteur dude's proposal to adopt the position at first reading, adopting the commission proposal adapted in accordance with the recommendations of the consultative working party of the legal services of the european parliament, the council and the commission.

written. ‒ the eesc is an advisory body of the european union. established in 1957, it provides expert advice to the eu's main institutions (the european commission, the european council and the european parliament). it does this by issuing 'opinions' on proposed eu legislative acts, as well as 'own-initiative opinions' on issues it considers needing to be addressed. one of its main tasks is to bridge the gap between the european institutions and 'organised civil society'. it promotes participatory democracy in the eu and helps to strengthen the role of civil society organisations by engaging in 'structured dialogue' with these groups in the eu member states as well as in other countries around the world.
written. ‒ cooperation with the committee of the regions, in particular through the competent committee in the european parliament, is institutionalised through the rules of procedure of the ep and is necessary for the exercise of the advisory function of that body.
written. ‒ the committee of the regions is an advisory body of the european union, because it conveys local and regional views to the eu institutions, which is of great importance to the eu, since the differences between member states, from the most obvious, such as the administrative division of the member states, their area and population, to the more complex, such as the structure of the administration, the autonomy of a region, traditions, the environment, the economy, etc., are large and need to be taken into account. the treaty of lisbon allows for decisions to be taken by consultation, requiring the cor to be consulted in the co-decision procedure when the european parliament is involved in a matter within its competence. the opinion of those closest to the electorate and those responsible for ensuring good living conditions for every eu citizen is important in order to deal more effectively with the specific issues that this level of governance must address. on the other hand, through consultations, the european institutions are introduced to the problems of regional authorities and are brought closer to the citizens themselves, thus establishing greater trust of the citizens in this great community of states. for all these reasons, i supported the decision to consult the committee of the regions on improving the functioning of the european union on the basis of the potential of the lisbon treaty.

‒ the committee of the regions is an advisory body representing local and regional authorities in the european union. the role of the committee of the regions is to express the views of local and regional authorities on eu legislation by publishing reports (opinions) on commission proposals. the committee of the regions is consulted by the commission, the council and the parliament before decisions are taken at eu level on issues relating to local and regional government (for example, employment policy, the environment, education or public health). under the lisbon treaty, the european commission must now consult local and regional authorities and their associations in the eu territory at a pre-legislative stage. the committee of the regions, as the representative of local and regional authorities, shall be actively involved in this procedure. the committee of the regions shall be consulted by the commission once it has drawn up a legislative proposal if the proposal relates to one of the many policy areas that have a direct impact on local and regional authorities.

madam president, tampering with the benchmarks is the same as stealing. so we need to restore confidence in benchmarks and we need to monitor their use well. the entire volume of eur 500 billion of financing instruments shows the importance of transparency. transparency of some data and methodology can resolve conflicts of interest. the reference interest rates are used, for example, to determine the variable part of a floating interest rate. this means that poorly, inadequately or intentionally miscalculated benchmarks can raise the overall interest rate of a consumer credit, ultimately putting consumers at a disadvantage. in croatia, we have seen this in the case of the swiss franc, which has brought many citizens and their families to the brink of ruin. it is important to establish a climate of trust, which is what this report should contribute to, and that is why i supported it.
madam president, i supported today the adoption of a regulation on indices used as benchmarks in financial instruments and financial contracts, because a single approach is crucial to preventing market fragmentation and the high-quality functioning of the single market is one of the key objectives at european union level. the objective is to prevent and avoid penalties, which occurred in december 2013 in the amount of eur 17 billion, all due to misinterpretation and manipulation of benchmarks, by means of a high-quality and clear regulatory approach. this regulation aims to improve the management system and avoid conflicts of interest and to improve the quality of input data and benchmarking methodologies, which is essential for the timely and high-quality resolution of compensation claims in the event of manipulation of benchmarks and input data.

written. ‒ i support the report by ms van nieuwenhuizen on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on indices used as benchmarks in financial instruments and financial contracts. the pricing of many financial instruments and financial contracts depends on the accuracy and correctness of benchmarks. serious cases of manipulation of benchmark interest rates, for example libor, euribor and benchmarks in the foreign exchange business sector, and alleged manipulation of benchmarks in the energy, oil and foreign exchange business sectors confirm that benchmarks can be subject to conflicts of interest and have discretionary rights systems and weak governance systems that are susceptible to manipulation. the inaccuracy and incorrectness of indices used as benchmarks, or the doubt as to their accuracy and correctness, can undermine market confidence, cause losses to consumers and investors and disrupt the real economy. it is therefore necessary to ensure the accuracy, stability and correctness of the benchmarks and the procedure for their establishment.
written. ‒ in order to avoid in the future the manipulation of reference interest rates, as was the case with libor and euribor, and the manipulation of benchmarks in the business sector, which can lead to a disturbance of market confidence, loss of consumers and investors and thus to disruption of the economy, i support this report because i believe that it is necessary to ensure the accuracy, stability and correctness of the benchmarks and the procedure for their establishment. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the establishment of a union-wide regulatory framework for benchmarks. this regulation would achieve transparency as to the purpose of the benchmark and input data on the basis of which any claims for compensation under national or union law can be effectively addressed. since the accuracy and reliability of a benchmark in measuring the economic reality for which it is intended depends on the methodology used and the input data, it is necessary to adopt a transparent methodology ensuring the reliability and accuracy of the benchmark.

written. ‒ small and medium-sized enterprises account for more than 98% of european enterprises, provide more than 67% of total employment in the union and 58% of gross value added; they are the backbone of the european union's economy and a key driver of long-term european economic growth and sustainable job creation in the 28 member states. employment in the environmental goods and services sector grew by 20% between 2007 and 2011, despite the crisis, and this sector offers opportunities for even greater economic activity and job creation for small and medium-sized enterprises (smes), including in areas affected by displacement and ageing populations. also, nine out of ten smes have 10 or fewer employees and these micro-enterprises account for 53% of all jobs in europe. all these data show the outstanding green growth potential of smes, which form the backbone of the european economy. i agree with the rapporteur who specifically points out the lack of access to adequate sources of risk capital, especially in the early stages, as one of the biggest constraints for the creation and development of growth-oriented enterprises, the appropriateness of the commission's action plan on improving access to finance for smes for only a small number of smes and the fact that financing alternatives should be developed by the private sector. i hope that the potential funding will be used through the european fund for strategic investments.

written. ‒ i voted against the report on green growth opportunities for smes, although i agree with the need to develop a green economy, because the draft report is nonspecific and ideologically written in relation to the action plan on which it should be based. i would point out that legislation is not the only obstacle to growth as the report states and that removing legislation would benefit eu citizens as well as small and medium-sized enterprises. the commission has also taken into account the fact that the union's contribution to the union's macro-financial assistance is limited to the minimum necessary to achieve the objectives of the union's macro-financial assistance. i also disagree with the parts of the report that call for the acceleration of the transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip) and its ratification. resource efficiency and the circular economy are opportunities for smes. it is necessary to ensure strong measures to help these companies to transition to a circular economy and i support the concrete proposals that we have managed to include in the resolution on behalf of the green/ees club.
written. ‒ i supported this report because of the importance of smes in the development of europe - smes account for more than 90% of european enterprises, they provide more than 67% of total employment in the union and 58% of gross value added, employment in the organic sector grew by 20% between 2007 and 2011. the global market for green goods is currently estimated at eur 1000 billion per year, which is expected to triple by 2020, with particular growth expected in the european union as a result of the green growth incentives for smes. the focus is mainly on high-tech enterprises directly implementing green innovation, but other enterprises need to be supported in complying with environmental regulations. i support the idea of green growth and circular economy and in this connection the use of renewable energy sources. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the conditions for the participation of third countries in union programmes in the field of research and technological development, in particular in the framework of the european research area. i think women's entrepreneurship needs to be strengthened in green growth and especially in rural areas.
written. ‒ i voted for the report on the possibilities of green growth for small and medium-sized enterprises, which in croatia are certainly not using their full potential. i come from a country where the business and investment climate is seriously damaged and where citizens witness the collapse of the national economy every day. i believe that micro, small and medium-sized enterprises are the key to economic recovery and can be harnessed by removing the barriers to the internal market that result from excessive regulation and bureaucratic procedures. i therefore support the proposal calling on the commission to refrain from further legislative provisions that will lead to unnecessary administrative burdens for businesses and for member states to take a responsible and clear approach to the interpretation of the rules in order to allow the green economy to fully develop and overcome obstacles related to financing and research, development, legal constraints and intergovernmental cooperation. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules and to monitor the implementation of the new rules.
vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– madam president, let me start by thanking everyone, and in particular the four rapporteurs, for the excellent work done on the reports – this is my personal opinion – but also for the very clear, determined way in which you have worked and also presented the reports today, but even more than that, for the ambitious approach. this is what we need at this moment. we all start by saying never before have we needed a more ambitious approach than we do now. well, i think it is time to translate this analysis, which is right, into action and i find your words, your work, your reports, and the overall attitude of this parliament in this respect extremely helpful in supporting an ambitious approach, including openly addressing some of the shortcomings that are the basis for changing and for delivering more of this sense of openness, of frankness, concerning the shortcomings and the needs we have to increase our level of ambition. it is also my approach, and that level of ambition that your reports are expressing is also my level of ambition in this field. as members have said, europe is facing multiple security challenges today and there is no doubt that we need to step up our common efforts in europe. i would say, in one sentence, that we need more defence in our european work and we need a more european approach in defence. this is the substance of what we are discussing here this afternoon. csdp and defence cooperation are crucial, yet they only work fully, they only unfold their full potential, if they are part of a comprehensive strategy, of a comprehensive policy, using all the instruments that we have as europeans, linking the external and internal dimension of our policies in an intelligent way. not only that – this is not the issue for debate this afternoon – we also need to use the tools that we have, including csdp, not only in reaction to events, but also in a strategic way to build security. building security is not only defence, it is also building the conditions for security worldwide and in particular in the regions around us: conflict prevention, development cooperation, promotion of human rights and democracy, coherence, economic and trade policies, including our own ones, even prevention and management of natural disasters and climate change. all of this is building security in the world, in the key areas in our neighbourhood and, at the end of the day, our own citizens’ security. this is going to be tackled in a systematic way when we discuss, in the european council at the end of june with heads of state and government, not only csdp but also our need for a new strategy, our strategic review. i will present in june the assessment i was asked and tasked to present on the global challenges we have in front of us, on the eu role in facing this. i hope that from there we will define and decide whether – or rather how – we need to develop a new european strategy to tackle the different and more challenging environment facing us. i think that the need to put together all the instruments we have is more obvious than ever in the challenges that we are facing in tackling the human tragedies that we see in the mediterranean sea. some of you mentioned that. finally we have started to mobilise all our efforts to prevent further loss of life at sea. i say finally, and i say finally in the european way. as one of these efforts, the european council at the end of april asked me to prepare a csdp operation to disrupt the business model of human trafficking networks across the mediterranean. yesterday, at the joint council meeting of foreign and defence ministers which i chaired, all member states agreed to establish a csdp operation to disrupt trafficking and smuggling networks. we took the decision yesterday to activate an operational headquarters and appoint an operational commander. there is still obviously some work to be done before the launch of this mission, namely on operational planning and on force generation. but let me say that the decision on establishing the operation being taken less than one month after the european council was asking, or tasking, for preparation on that is an absolute record. i was told that it normally takes six to ten months to take the decision to establish an operation. i know that time is not in itself an element of evaluation, but in this case time is an element of urgency that we need to face, especially when summer is coming. so i have to say that i think that this is the best way of addressing the issue of better and more effective csdp in europe, specifically using the instruments we have on the basis of the situations we are facing on a day-to-day basis. let me remind you in this hemicycle that it is exactly one month today since we faced that tragedy in the mediterranean sea when 700 to 800 hundred people died. it is still not enough, we still have a lot more work to do in different areas, but i think that for the first time we can say that we have a quick and european response to this crisis. still, the preparation of a csdp mission in the mediterranean and the reinforcement of the existing csdp mission, especially the one in niger that was decided last week, are only two elements, important ones but only two elements of our strategy to tackle this challenge. last week the commission presented the european agenda on migration – which this house will be debating tomorrow – outlining the immediate measures to respond to the crisis in the mediterranean, both on the humanitarian and on the security side, and the steps to be taken, both immediate ones and the long-term ones. let me stress here that no member state can be left alone – should not be left alone – to face the huge migratory pressure, as this is a european responsibility. i think that finally we are beginning to realise that. the way forward is, and will still be, hard and long, but we are probably now starting to realise that. we are finally proposing a european response which has never been the case before: combining internal and external policies, working together as europeans on the immediate humanitarian emergency, on the security situation, as well as the root causes in countries of origin and transit. tackling the root causes means tackling poverty, unequal access to resources, be they natural or financial, tackling conflicts, crises and the violation of human rights; conflicts and crises, starting obviously with libya, and the support we are giving to the dialogue led by bernardino león. this is specifically what ‘comprehensive approach’ means. to me the point is to make this comprehensive approach – which i understand is also sometimes criticised in the danjean report – real, to make it happen, to make it work, using all the instruments that we have – and they are many – and achieving more coherence among the different instruments and the way we are using them. we need that more than ever. since december 2013, when the european leaders took some decisions on security and defence, you have all said that the security situation in and around the european union has changed dramatically. it has clearly not changed in a positive way. the concurrency, intensity, frequency and complexity of conflicts and crises in our neighbourhood is unique and the speed with which this has happened is even more unique. that is also why we need to seriously rethink our way of building security while we manage the urgency of current crises. that is also why we need a strategy to move ahead. the demand for the european union to act as a provider of security is increasing and will, most probably, continue to increase. we will only be able to respond to this demand in a credible way if we make the csdp more effective and if we make sure we have the right kinds of capabilities, which in turn needs a solid, defence industrial base. the european council in june will be an occasion to take stock of progress in this regard and to show the way ahead. i have just presented my report to the foreign affairs council, ahead of the june council, and simultaneously the commission delivered its report on the implementation of its 2013 defence communication. both documents register progress in most areas where the european council in 2013 set tasks, and point to areas where we need, and we can have, further progress. i would say we need, we can and we must have further progress. we worked on this just yesterday, as you mentioned, with the defence and foreign ministers together, putting together – this is also a comprehensive approach – different sides of our csdp work. among the achievements i can mention, we have the adoption of the eu’s first comprehensive maritime strategy and action plan, or the cyber policy framework. i would like to mention specifically one element: the security development nexus. on this, i think we learned an important lesson from the csdp training missions in somalia, in mali and in niger, which is that the troops we train must often be supplied with equipment – tents, uniforms, radios, basic infrastructure. at the end of april the commission adopted a joint communication based on my proposal to enable the european union to train and equip the forces of local partners. it was addressed to the council and to parliament and i count on your support to take this forward, as it would be an extremely relevant and precious step. being completely frank, as you are, there are also areas where the picture is much less encouraging. i am thinking of rapid response where the lack of political will has so far made it impossible to move. i know this is frustrating for many members of this parliament. it is frustrating for me, as well. force generation, too, is problematic. i raised this with ministers yesterday in a very clear and open way. if we take decisions then we need to translate them into action. this is a matter of being operational, this is also a matter of credibility, and this means taking responsibilities in the member states with concrete decisions to follow up on force generation. i also know that some of you are very eager to see the full potential of csdp-related articles of the lisbon treaty fully used. the relevant sections of mr danjeanʼs report are very precious in this regard and let me say that i am completely determined to work with your support, with your help, to build the political conditions for having this done. progress has also remained limited on csdp financing more broadly. indeed, the tension between our level of ambition and the level of resources has grown even bigger. the kukan and tarand report rightly raises a number of issues for both civilian and military csdp financing. on cost saving and efficiency measures in civilian missions: we will continue working with the commission to facilitate a faster deployment of civilian missions and improvements in the financial management. in that context, i would like to stress the importance of sufficient payment appropriations for the cfsp budget. on financing of military operations, the review of the athena mechanism took place recently. a new council decision was adopted at the end of march. while largely inconclusive, these debates will continue. i am ready, and most of all i am willing, to support and to lead the debate among member states and, i hope, to lead it to some results. this is going to be key. the question of burden-sharing among member states, which is what this question is, is crucial and needed if we are to face a future – and hopefully also a present – csdp that really works. as the demand for csdp will remain high, we also need to fill our defence capability gaps. at a time of reduced public spending, the pooling and sharing of capacities and resources, especially of high-end capabilities, is more than ever a recipe that can reconcile possibilities and needs in this regard. we have made some important steps toward implementing collaborative projects. we agreed back in 2013 on air-to-air refuelling capacity, remotely piloted craft systems, satellite communications and cyber. their development, notably on the first of these projects, is now in an advanced stage but i made it very clear to the ministers yesterday that we also need to embark on new collaborative projects. we have to bring forward the ones that we already have, and we need to put new ones on the table. this parliament has calculated – as you said, we do not need to be imaginative, we need to read the things that we already know and make them real – that the cost of non-europe in defence amounts to some eur 26 billion per year, an enormous amount of money, especially in these times, and more than that, as we are all politicians in this room, 70% of european citizens support more integration in defence. this is the clearest call for action that we could receive and i count on your support. count, please, on my full determination to make this real, to have more european integration in defence. we also need to spend better, and better together. this is a crucial point, especially in these times of austerity, and we need to focus on the output. we need to invest too in our partnerships. the one with nato – that is essential. hybrid, non-linear risks: i have put a premium on enhanced cooperation and contingency planning. if the old debate on a nato-eu rivalry ever had any sense it does not anymore; it does not make any sense in these times. i was happy to welcome the nato secretary-general, jens stoltenberg, yesterday at our ministerial meeting, just as i was happy to be at the foreign ministers nato meeting last week in antalya. our cooperation is increasing, not only our cooperation at the highest political level, but staff-to-staff cooperation is also going on very well. we are different in nature, but we have some common points on the agenda that we can coordinate and cooperate on. the other extremely relevant cooperation we have to invest in is the one with the united nations. all member states have just agreed on a new action plan to announce eu support for un peacekeeping, and the un secretary general ban ki-moon will be at the foreign affairs council on 22 june. we need to work on different aspects on different levels, as your reports clearly identify. the gomes report on the impact of developments in european defence markets on the security and defence capabilities in europe indicates that the competitiveness of the european defence industry is a priority, and i fully support this. a strong competitive european defence industrial base needs more cooperation between member states, a more efficient internal market, more robust security of supply guarantees, competitive and integrated supply chains, and support for research and innovation. a healthy industrial base is indeed key in support of any credible defence policy as, among others, it generates cutting-edge programmes, innovation with spillover effects into the civilian domain and vice versa, and a highly skilled workforce that accounts for 400 000 direct and 960 000 indirect jobs across europe. at the same time, our industry faces a wide range of challenges both at the global and at the european level: increasingly globalised supply chains, increased defence of said demands, global shifts in defence spending. our ratio regarding r&d investment is 1:7 as compared to the us but, and this is the news, 1:3 in comparison with the so-called brics. the plunge in defence r&d since 2006, more than 29% in real terms, is detrimental to much needed innovation in europe and puts at risk our capability in producing defence equipment and the competitiveness of our industry. the european industrial landscape remains characterised by a fragmented demand side, a plethora of national programmes and variance of equipment, generating high costs for industry. increasingly integrated civilian military supply chains with a growing reliance on civilian technologies means that companies more and more rely on civil production in terms of turnover and revenues. if nothing is done, we could face the risk in the longer term of having a lower level of technological sophistication due to slower rates of innovation. we could also face decreasing competitiveness with the ultimate loss of production capacities and jobs and thus increasing dependence on foreign supplies – and we are talking about the european union. the gomes report also highlights the need for a full and correct implementation of the two defence directives of 2009 with a view to opening up the defence market chains for companies from all over europe. an open and transparent european defence equipment market is a precondition for our defence companies to access european supply chains in view of building strategic and sustainable alliances with european partners. i fully share the objective to ensure the effective implementation of the defence procurement and the defence transfers directives. the commission has started evaluating the defence directives and in 2016 will report to parliament and council on their implementation and on whether they have achieved their objectives. in december 2013, heads of state and government called for more investment in cooperative research programmes, more synergies between defence and civil research, as well as for a preparatory action on csdp-related research to be set up. here we have three avenues. first, collaborative defence r&t. the european defence agency (eda) has a longstanding track record in defence r&t projects and programmes. second, dual-use research, and third, the establishment of the preparatory action on csdp-related research, a potential game-changer testing the viability of defence-oriented and csdp-related research at european union level. the commission has the lead here, but the eda, having long experience in defence r&t, can provide support. joint commission-eda workshops with stakeholders to discuss the modalities, content and the process to establish such a preparatory action, are paving the way. another potential game-changer could be the council mandate on developing a european union-wide security and supply regime. security of supply is essential for the sustainment of operations, the development of long-term planning and cooperation, and the functioning of the internal market for defence. we expect the roadmap for the comprehensive eu-wide security of supply regime in early 2016. to conclude, let me thank you for the work you have done, for the work of this parliament in general on csdp, and also on the preparation for the june council. i know you have been working very hard and intensively on this and this is extremely helpful. let me conclude by mentioning those 7 000 men and women who are currently deployed under the eu flag in military and civilian missions under dangerous and difficult conditions, from afghanistan to somalia, from mali to the central african republic. i want to end my comments today by saluting the work of men and women deployed in the field under the eu flag and thank them for what they are doing. this is what we should remember all the time: that our discussions, our decisions, are then translated in their work on a daily basis, in very difficult conditions, for the security of our citizens, the stability of the regions where they are deployed and peace in our world. written. i welcome this document because it is a good step forward for the member states of the european union to share responsibility for migration in a way that is solidarity-based. commitments on paper must now be honoured in practice. member states must demonstrate their ability to find common solutions to the mass influx of migrants, but this solution cannot be focused on the eu alone. it is therefore important for countries in transition and countries of origin to align their approach to prevent traffickers from transporting migrants to the eu. it is also important to carry out information campaigns in the host countries to discourage potential migrants from travelling, as it has been shown that almost two thirds of asylum applications are rejected and that migrants, after having undergone an extremely difficult and expensive journey, are ultimately returned to the countries from which they came in the vast majority of cases. it also showed that development aid from the eu to third countries is certainly not well targeted because it does not improve the quality of life of the local population, who then literally put their lives on the line to find a better life. the document represents a significant step forward in the response to the tragedies in the mediterranean and, if adopted, will reflect solidarity among member states.
written. the crisis is a reality for many citizens of the member states. however, millions of people live in much more brutal conditions in our immediate neighborhood. for them, and the eu, the troubled one is a promised land compared to the desperation from which they must flee. refugees are victims of a triple threat: devastation in their home countries, the greed of human traffickers, and the front lines of rejection in the countries where they want to continue living. refugees must not remain a problem only for the member states whose borders and coasts they reach. the commission reacted quickly. the council with some hesitation. the differences are in the extent to which the commission defends the common european interests and the council represents the interests of the member states. the eu has taken in one million of the world's 12 million refugees. lebanon, a country of 6 million people, has 1.2 million refugees. if the union is to be judged by how it treats the most needy in society, and migrants certainly are, then we need to seriously review current migration policies and fundamentally reform them. that is why i support the commission's proposals.
written. migration has become a major concern for the eu following the large wave of refugees and migrants arriving in europe by land or by boat across the mediterranean sea. in the first two months of 2015 alone, 26,600 illegal border crossings were recorded, as well as 1829 casualties at sea border crossings. the commission has therefore set up a new european agenda on migration, which sets common policy objectives for the 28 member states to adopt criteria and legislate on migration. the current system cannot cope with the increasing influx of migrants, which is further empowered and accelerated by the profits made by smugglers from numerous war-torn areas, which encourage people to flee and where the basic human rights that migrants should have are not respected. the commission therefore proposes mandatory quotas for member states to relocate the many migrants who have managed to reach the eu, so that the first countries to be hit do not bear the full burden of asylum, namely italy, greece and malta. the new mechanism is based on the size of the member state, gdp, unemployment rate and number of existing asylum applications.

written. ‒ for the proper functioning of the internal market, cross-border insolvency proceedings should be conducted in an efficient and effective manner. the activities of entrepreneurs have increasingly cross-border effects and are increasingly regulated by union law for the same reason. at the same time, the insolvency of such undertakings affects the proper functioning of the internal market and there is a need for a union act requiring the coordination of measures taken in respect of the assets of the insolvent debtor. therefore, bearing in mind that the proposed insolvency regulation seeks to increase the efficiency of cross-border insolvency proceedings in order to ensure the smooth functioning of the internal market and its resilience in economic crises, and that this objective is also in line with the current political priorities of the european union on promoting economic recovery and sustainable growth as well as higher investment and preserving employment, as set out in the europe 2020 strategy, and on protecting the development and survival of enterprises, as set out in the small business act, i have supported this recommendation for a second reading on the council position at first reading with a view to the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on a common procedure.
written. ‒ having regard to the council's position at first reading (16636/5/2014 c8-0090/2015), to the opinion of the european economic and social committee of 22 may 2013 and to the recommendation for second reading of the committee on legal affairs (a8-0155/2015), i accept this recommendation for second reading.
written. ‒i voted in favour of this council position at first reading for the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on insolvency proceedings. in particular, this regulation seeks to further promote a 'rescue culture' in the eu. the main elements of this regulation are the extension of the scope of the regulation to include 'preventive' insolvency proceedings aimed at rescuing undertakings, but also to cover a wider range of personal insolvency proceedings. the criteria for jurisdiction are also clarified and the procedural framework for assessing jurisdiction is improved. the establishment of a system of tax insolvency registers will increase transparency for debtors. this regulation enhances the prospects of rescuing companies by avoiding the initiation of secondary proceedings where the interests of local creditors are otherwise safeguarded and provides a legal framework for the coordination of the proceedings of members of a group of companies. it is necessary to include an additional measure to counter the phenomenon of consumers abusing the possibility of obtaining a more favourable legal position by changing jurisdiction.
written. ‒ i voted for the amendment of the insolvency regulation to focus on cross-border proceedings. the regulation lays down new rules with a set of measures aimed at preventing abuse of position in order to ensure a more favourable legal position for debtors who, for certain reasons, have become over-indebted, insolvent or illiquid. i therefore agree with the decision that member states are obliged to display the relevant data in cases of cross-border insolvency proceedings through the electronic register, which will improve transparency but also facilitate their implementation. but as a representative of a country with a sad history of over 19 000 companies that have become bankrupt, i believe that we must focus on measures that allow for the restructuring of debtors at a stage where debtors are unable to make payments because they are unable to meet their due-value obligations. the essence of bankruptcy proceedings should be the fair distribution of assets, but unfortunately we are witnessing different examples. the commission has also concluded that the measures in question constitute state aid within the meaning of article 107 (1) of the treaty.

written. ‒ i supported the report by mep iuliu winkler on the establishment of a union system for self-certification of responsible importers of tin, tantalum and tungsten, their ores and gold originating from conflict-affected and high-risk areas by applying due diligence in the supply chain. the objective is to establish a union system of supply chain due diligence self-certification to restrict the opportunities for armed groups and security forces to trade in tin, tantalum and tungsten, their ores and gold, and to ensure transparency and security of supply for importers, smelters and refiners sourcing from conflict-affected and high-risk areas. the commission should be able to assess the impact of the measures taken by the member states on the implementation of the union's macro-financial assistance. in these areas, breaking the links between conflict and illegal mineral exploitation is crucial for peace and stability.
written. ‒ i consider it unacceptable that the european union, through the unregulated market in minerals and metals, by trading in these activities and by financing armed groups, indirectly participates and encourages the continuation of the conflict in these areas. the activities of these armed groups are linked to many grave violations of human rights, especially of women and children. since the foundation on which the european union rests is precisely this principle - respect for human rights, it is logical that this community of ours should not be a conscious participant in supporting something that does not agree with these principles. i believe that the process of self-certification of importers, with the involvement of a supervisory body that will monitor the correctness of the implementation of the process itself, will contribute to reducing criminal acts in the areas mentioned and that it is necessary to reach an agreement on the open issues as soon as possible.
written. ‒ natural mineral resources in conflict-affected and high-risk areas, despite their high development potential, can be a source of dispute, with revenues generated from them being disrupted by the outbreak or continuation of violent conflict, undermining efforts towards development, good governance and the rule of law. in these areas, breaking the links between conflict and illegal mineral exploitation is a key element in ensuring peace, development and stability. human rights violations are common in the extractive industry and may include child labour, sexual violence, forced disappearance, forced displacement and destruction of sites of ritual and cultural importance. i therefore support the report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing a union system for the self-certification of responsible importers of tin, tantalum and tungsten, their ores and gold originating in conflict-affected and high-risk areas by the due diligence approach in the supply chain and the adoption of the commission proposal at first reading.
written. ‒ i support the report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing a union system for self-certification of responsible importers of tin, tantalum and tungsten, their ores and gold originating in conflict-affected and high-risk areas through due diligence in the supply chain. mineral-rich countries affected by conflict are in a vicious circle where the rebels are financed by valuable mineral resources. to stop this, international organisations and the ep have called for a due diligence system between excavation companies and importers. the proposal covers 3t and g tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold, the participation of companies is voluntary, it covers any conflict affected area and it covers melting and processing companies as well as importers. importers wishing to participate may declare themselves as responsible importers of a member state and must comply with the proposed measures. it is accepted that the areas of conflict are strictly defined and that voluntary participation is mandatory for importers and for producers.
written. - i think it's important to remove the link between the mineral and the conflict. i also want to stress that we need a regulation that is applicable and appropriate. we need mandatory certification for mills and mineral processors, and we need to encourage mills and processors outside the eu to do business responsibly by including importers in the mandatory certification scheme. however, going beyond certification could be counterproductive, as it would not only be a burden for industry in the eu, but also for developing countries. we must not restrict access to the eu market for them, as this could cause job losses in underdeveloped countries. this should not be the aim of a european union regulation. by introducing applicable and appropriate certification rules for smelters and refiners, and importers of minerals and metals, we will create a system that is applicable and effective in the effort to break the link between minerals and conflict.
written. ‒ the profits from the trade in minerals with high development potential are often used to finance armed conflict and i agree that we must not allow this harmful practice to continue. it is also of particular importance in countries affected by conflict or identified as high-risk areas to dismantle the link between conflict and illicit mineral exploitation. many member states are indeed dependent on imports of these ores and metals found in electrical appliances, which we use in our daily lives. however, they cannot agree with the basic intention of the regulation which seeks to establish a self-certification system in a manner that treats due diligence in the supply chain in order to restrict the opportunities for armed groups and security forces to trade in tin, tantalum, tungsten, their ores and gold. the commission notes that the measures are not intended to create a situation in which the union industry would be able to compete with the union industry. i consider that such a requirement would impose costs and unnecessary administrative burdens which would ultimately affect the competitiveness of smes which do not need the additional burden and therefore i voted against it.
written. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution on a commission delegated directive amending, for the purposes of adapting to technical progress, annex iii to directive 2011/65eu of the european parliament and of the council as regards the exemption for the use of cadmium in lighting and display lighting, rejecting the delegated act of the european commission on the grounds that the exemption from the ban on cadmium for certain led lamps and displays is inadmissible. cadmium is a highly toxic substance that should have been completely banned by 2014, especially as alternatives that do not involve the use of cadmium have been developed in the meantime. i consider that the exemption of the use of cadmium, which was extended until mid-2017 for light bulbs and until mid-2018 for screens, would encourage unnecessary entry into the eu market of products containing that substance. therefore, i object to such a solution.
written. ‒ cadmium (cd) is a silvery-white, soft and plastic metal that can be cut with a knife, drawn into wires and forged into sheets, and is used to coat other metals, especially iron and steel. because of the toxicity of cadmium and its compounds, and with the development of environmental awareness, cadmium is being phased out and replaced by replacement materials. directive 2011/65/eu on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment limits, inter alia, the use of cadmium in electrical and electronic equipment, but also provides for exemptions from the restriction. i supported the objection to the commission delegated directive amending the annex to adapt it to technical progress as regards the exemption for the use of cadmium in lighting and display lighting. the commission notes that the use of cadmium in screens will have a beneficial effect due to their low energy consumption and that cadmium-free quantum dots are not yet technically available. the resolution calls for the derogation to be repealed and for the commission to submit a new delegated act which will take into account the parliament's position, given that technological developments are now producing displays which do not contain toxic cadmium.
written. ‒ the toxic properties of cadmium are the reason for its inclusion in the list of directive 2011/65/eu on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment. the commission's delegated directive is amazing, and so are the days of explanation in the preamble to the act. i consider that the reasons for the exemption to limit the use of cadmium in lighting and display lighting are not valid or justified. the commission notes that the exemption granted to the applicant is not limited to the product concerned, but also to the product concerned. in my country we would rightly call this a conciliation procedure, which is borderline legal or even illegal if incorrect data or wrongly reasoned reasons are given to push through a legislative act. i therefore support the adoption of this resolution and would indeed ask the commission to explain the reasons for adopting this delegated directive.
written. ‒ i support the motion for a resolution on amending, for the purpose of adapting to technical progress, annex iii to directive 2011/65/eu of the european parliament and of the council as regards the exemption for cadmium in lighting and display lighting applications by asking the commission to submit a new delegated act to take account of parliament's position. in accordance with article 5 (a) (1), exemptions shall be included in annex iii, provided that they do not compromise the protection of the environment and health as provided for in regulation (ec) no 1907/2006 and if any of the following conditions are met: their elimination or replacement by design changes or by materials and components not requiring any of the materials or substances listed in annex ii is not feasible for scientific or technical reasons; the reliability of the replacement substances cannot be guaranteed; or the overall adverse effects on the environment, health and safety of the consumer of the replacement are likely to outweigh the overall adverse effects on the environment, health and safety of the consumer of the replacement. the commission also found that the exemption for lighting was not justified on the basis of the information available at that time and therefore explicitly opposed it.

terrorism, to the top of the agenda in ethiopia, and the government has expressed an interest in expanding cooperation on these matters with the european union. on climate change, ethiopia’s policy in global discussion is in line with the european union position. the european union intends to sign the lima declaration on cooperation with ethiopia, as several eu member states have already done. in fruit in terms of progress towards the millennium development goals for social and economic growth. the imf estimate for economic growth in the current year, 2015, is 7.5-8.5%, which is rather impressive for the region. moreover, according to a recent report by the world bank, poverty in ethiopia fell by one third between 2000 and 2011. these are remarkable achievements and i am glad that our support contributed to them. but we all know there is another side to the coin: as in many post-conflict situations, democratic transition in ethiopia is taking time and does not always go smoothly. the commission is well aware that the political environment is not conducive to transparent, credible and inclusive elections – and this is a concern which we have raised with the government full respect for freedom of speech, freedom of association and freedom of the press, as provided for by the ethiopian constitution. the government’s line is that their primary concern is stability and security for their people, and that they cannot permit destabilisation of the country which would jeopardise social and economic progress. thus, we cannot say that we agree on everything, but we have an ongoing open dialogue on these issues, sometimes with constructive results. we are, for example, discussing the possibility of cooperating on improving the quality of the ethiopian media, both public and private, as an outcome of a recent article 8 dialogue on the media. turning to the elections, you are all aware that progress in following up implementation of the recommendations of previous election observation missions has been lacking. the reports of 2005 and 2010 have unfortunately been rejected. we have not received an invitation for the elections that will take place next sunday, and therefore the european union will not send an election observation mission. similarly, we have decided against financially supporting the undp electoral programme. the situation of journalists, bloggers, members of the opposition and other individuals is a major cause for concern. they have been imprisoned for having expressed their opinions publicly. the space for the media and political parties has been gradually reduced since just before the start of the electoral period in 2014. the eu delegation, together with member states present in addis ababa, is closely following the situation and monitors all the relevant trials. we also discuss these issues, including the use of the anti-terrorism proclamation to stifle dissent, with the ethiopian authorities, and the population continues to face, as discussed in the human rights subcommittee meetings in january this year and in september 2014, when the eu issued a statement on the political and human rights situation in ethiopia. we will certainly continue to follow the situation closely and to react publicly when necessary. i will be happy to hear your views on eu engagement with ethiopia.

member of the commission.– mr president, i welcome the opportunity to discuss eu development aid to eritrea in the light of documented human rights abuses. respect for human rights is a basic principle of eu foreign policy and therefore features regularly in our dialogue with partners in the entire world, including eritrea. in this dialogue, and also publically, we raise our concerns that eritrea continues to violate its obligations and does not respect fundamental human rights. we urge concrete gestures such as the liberation of the prisoners – notably mr dawit isaak, an eu-eritrean citizen – who have been detained incommunicado since 2001. the european union also raises those concerns in international forums, notably at meetings of the un human rights council, where we appeal to eritrea to cooperate with the un special rapporteur and the un commission of inquiry for eritrea and to give them access to eritrea. that said, it is our belief that continued engagement with eritrea is the best option for a number of reasons. firstly, engagement creates the possibility to stress the need for concrete changes and progress across the board, and to insist on the importance of adhering to international standards on human rights. isolation rarely helps in these circumstances. secondly, engagement allows us to continue supporting the population and improving living conditions. lastly, engagement contributes to peace and stability in the country and the wider region. some minor progress has recently been achieved: for example, in december 2014 the government of eritrea announced that the previously indefinite duration of national service would be limited to 18 months for new recruits. this is an important decision, since the open-ended duration of national service was a major push factor in migration. the decision now needs to be implemented. we must do what we can to alleviate the huge stress upon eritrea’s population. they are facing a problematic food security situation and a lack of economic prospects and opportunities. the sharpest evidence of their despair is the outflow of people, especially young people, many of whom venture on a dangerous journey, trying to enter the eu by illegal means, and are easy prey for traffickers. that is why european union development projects currently being implemented under the 10th european development fund (edf), in the amount of eur 53.7 million and covering the period from 2008 to now, relate mainly to agriculture and food security. the second sector is governance, with the focus on capacity-building and access to justice at grassroots level, in particular through community courts. our aid is provided through projects and not through budget support. strict monitoring procedures ensure that eu aid directly benefits the people, creates jobs and reduces poverty. there is no support to the central government in eritrea. as regards the programming of the aid under the 11th european development fund, discussions are ongoing. it is proposed that eu development aid will support social and economic development, including through increasing access to renewable energy, in order to achieve tangible results for the population such as the creation of more jobs and the improvement of people’s livelihoods in eritrea. in addition, support for governance-related activities that would promote sustainable economic growth is also provided for. apart from the eu cooperation financed from the european development fund, the european union has also allocated thematic funds in order to support, and build the capacity of, formal and informal civil society organisations active in the areas of social, cultural and economic rights. although the context currently allows for only limited visibility, this engagement with non-state actors does encourage plurality and will strengthen citizens’ participation, including in the medium and long term. let me say, too, a few words about migration. eritrea is a key country of origin. by improving the livelihoods of the people of eritrea, development aid is addressing and will continue to address the root causes of migration. eritrea is an active partner in the khartoum process, under which human rights issues related to migrants and refugees will be addressed, as agreed in the ministerial declaration signed in rome on 28 november 2014. our development aid should also be seen in a regional context. through regional projects the european union is linking eritrea better to the region. recent developments in yemen are of particular concern and may have serious implications for the stability of the region and of eritrea, which is located just across the red sea from yemen. the eu support for the population enables people to be less vulnerable to radicalisation, and eu aid should thus also be seen as contributing to peace and stability in the region. i would be happy to hear your views on eu engagement with eritrea.

madam president, each year the percentage of the reduction in direct payments is set aside in the reserve for agricultural crises. the commission has also proposed that the amount of direct payments in 2016 for 2015 be reduced by 1,39% per farmer for support above eur 2 000, thereby providing for an amount of eur 441,6 million to be set aside in the crisis reserve. i am personally opposed, as are many of my colleagues, to the use of this reserve to repair the damage suffered by farmers for political reasons, for which funds must be provided at the level of the whole budget and not just from the agricultural budget lines. in the event of natural disasters and emergencies, epidemics and similar crises, this reserve will be of enormous importance for the recovery of agriculture. the republic of croatia and our farmers are exempt from this allocation for the crisis reserve, because we still do not use 100% of the amount.

written. ‒ i voted in favour of the draft legislative resolution of the european parliament on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council fixing the adjustment rate for direct payments provided for in council regulation (eu) no 1306/2013 for 2015, because of the importance and the support it gives to the agricultural sector, which is facing serious difficulties. the situation on the world market requires the establishment of a crisis fund to provide concrete support and security for european farmers. farmers need to feel the real solidarity of the european union in order to regain their confidence and strengthen european agriculture. however, it is important to ensure that croatian, but also bulgarian and romanian farmers have access to certain measures of assistance and financing in case of crisis.
written. ‒ agriculture and farmers today face many challenges that are becoming increasingly difficult to cope with. from market disturbances, which have been 'salted to the ground' by the russian embargo and the abolition of milk quotas, to climate change and nature, which reacts unpredictably every now and then and leaves severe consequences for the food production sector. the decision to set up a crisis fund is therefore justified and i supported it, as it will be able to intervene when necessary and help affected farmers in the most acute crises. i believe that this fund should not finance compensation for farmers who suffered as a result of the russian embargo, but that money should be taken from the eu general budget reserve for this purpose, given that the russian embargo is the result of a political decision and has no causes in the agricultural sector.
written. ‒ since farmers applying for direct payments for one calendar year (n) receive payments within a certain payment period in the financial year (n + 1). in addition, member states may make late payments to farmers after the expiry of that payment period, within certain time limits. those late payments may be made in the following financial year. where financial discipline is applied in a given calendar year, the adjustment rate should not apply to payments for which aid applications are submitted in calendar years in which financial discipline is not applied. therefore, in order to ensure equal treatment of farmers, it is appropriate to provide that the adjustment rate should only apply to payments for which aid applications are submitted in the calendar year in which financial discipline applies, irrespective of when the payment to farmers is made. i therefore support the rapporteur's opinion adopting the first reading position on the fixing of the adjustment rate for direct payments provided for in council regulation (eu) no 1306/2013 for the calendar year 2015.
written. ‒ i supported the report of my colleague, mr ašeriski, on the adjustment rate for direct payments for 2015. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the establishment of a reserve to be set aside at the beginning of each year to provide support to the agricultural sector in the event of major crises affecting agricultural production or distribution, such as the russian embargo, by applying a reduction in direct payments under the financial discipline mechanism. the amount of the reserve for crises in the agricultural sector envisaged to be included in the commission's draft budget for 2016 is eur 441,6 million in current prices and the percentage of the adjustment rate for financial discipline is 1,393041%, which is calculated taking into account the fact that it will only apply to amounts of direct payments per farmer exceeding eur 2000 and not in all member states. in this context, it should be noted that bulgaria, romania and croatia are in the process of phasing in direct payments in the calendar year 2015 and are as such exempted from financial discipline.
written. ‒ i support this report on the agricultural sector on the slight reduction in the amount of direct payments. it is necessary that the reserve for providing additional support to the agricultural sector in the event of major crises affecting agricultural production or distribution is established at the beginning of each year in order to ensure that the annual financial ceilings for financing market related expenditure and direct payments are respected, in accordance with articles 25 and 26 of regulation (eu) no 1306/2013 of the european parliament and of the council.
written. ‒ i support this initiative to slightly reduce the amount of direct payments to help farmers and the agricultural sector in the european union in cases of major crises. it is important to note that these adjustments apply only to direct payments granted to farmers in the corresponding calendar year exceeding eur 2 000. in addition, in order to ensure equal treatment of all farmers, the adjustment rate will only apply to payments for which aid applications are submitted in the calendar year in which the financial discipline applies, irrespective of when the payment to farmers is made. furthermore, as a result of the gradual introduction of direct payments, the adjustment rate applies to bulgaria and romania only from 1 january 2016 and to croatia, which i represent in this parliament, only from 1 january 2022. in the other member states, the amount of the reduction in direct payments for the calendar year 2015 will be reduced by only 1,39%.

written. ‒ i support the accession of the republic of croatia to the convention on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, because the eu borders are closed to individuals, but not to authorities such as the police, prosecution authorities and courts. for these reasons, i agree that the accession will contribute to the direct transmission of requests for mutual assistance between the judicial authorities of the member states, allow a better exchange of information between the member states while respecting the procedures of the requesting state. the purpose of this convention is to give effect to the principle of mutual recognition of judgments on the freezing of property and of evidence for the purposes of criminal proceedings between member states. the enforcement of fines in a member state other than that in which the fine was imposed has also been facilitated. the establishment of joint investigation teams between two or more countries involved in the investigation will also help in the fight against criminal activities.

‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) was created to provide additional support to workers affected by the consequences of major structural changes in world trade flows. the annual budget available for the egf in 2015 amounts to eur 150 million, of which, in accordance with article 11 (1) of the egf regulation, 0,5% (eur 811,825 in 2015) may be made available, on the initiative of the commission, for technical assistance to finance a range of activities ranging from preparation, monitoring, data collection and development of basic knowledge to audit, control and evaluation activities necessary for the implementation of the egf regulation. the report proposes to mobilise eur 630.000, representing approximately 0,39% of the maximum annual budget available for the egf in 2015, to finance the expert group of egf contact persons and the egf implementation seminar. it is important to increase general awareness of the egf and its visibility and to enhance communication between all parties involved in the application for mobilisation of the egf, in particular the social partners and stakeholders at regional and local level, all with a view to achieving the greatest possible synergies. in the light of the above, i supported the report by mr depreza on the proposal for a decision of the european parliament and of the council on the mobilisation of the egf in the field of cooperation on budgetary matters and sound financial management.

‒ the european union solidarity fund was set up following the major floods in central europe in the summer of 2002 to help member states recover from the consequences of large-scale natural disasters. the fund has up to eur 500 million available per year. i support the report by mep siegfried mureșan on the activation of the fund in the amount of eur 66,5 million for assistance to romania, bulgaria and italy. the commission has also received a request from the member states to provide assistance to the commission in the event of major floods in the spring, summer and autumn of 2014. the republic of croatia, more precisely the eastern part, was also affected by floods in the spring of 2014. this year, the solidarity fund has allocated 8.9 million euros to help the area, but the money is intended for the rehabilitation of public infrastructure, but not family homes, of which more than 2,000 have been destroyed according to official figures. we are increasingly victims of elementary disasters that we cannot prevent, so we need to discuss and design preventive systems that would reduce the potential damage.
written. ‒ in late july last year, bulgaria and romania were hit by a major flood that took five lives. in november, a similar fate befell italy after a severe storm forced the evacuation of thousands of people who were left homeless. it is precisely situations like this, where people lose their loved ones and their homes, that require the existence of a fund that will respond quickly. at such times, people need compassion and solidarity, but first and foremost, material help. the european union solidarity fund (eusf) was therefore established to respond effectively to such unforeseeable situations. it was created in response to the floods in central europe in the summer of 2002, since then it has been used for 67 disasters including floods, forest fires, earthquakes, storms and droughts. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 26 to supplement this regulation by laying down detailed rules for the application of this regulation. the importance of this fund is also indisputable, as the consequences of the elementary disasters must be remedied as soon as possible to prevent further suffering of the victims. in view of all the above, and further encouraged by last year's catastrophic floods in croatia, when the assistance from this fund helped the inhabitants of the županja plain to rebuild that area of croatia, i supported this decision with the wish that the lives of the affected inhabitants of bulgaria, romania and italy be normalized as soon as possible.

written. ‒ following the revelation of non-transparent and unfair tax treatment by certain member states of large international companies, which undermined the tax bases of other member states and the eu's single market, the european parliament set up a special committee on tax rulings and other measures similar in nature or effect (taxe) in strasbourg on 12 february. the taxe committee aims to examine tax rules, state aid schemes and similar measures in all member states from 1991 to the present, and to organise hearings involving representatives of the european commission responsible for tax issues, representatives of member states' tax administrations, the private sector and representatives of other interested groups to help find solutions to unfair tax practices and aggressive tax planning. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the establishment of a european data protection supervisor, the appointment of a european data protection supervisor and the appointment of a european data protection supervisor. as the ep supported the establishment of the taxe committee and its six-month mandate in february, i supported the extension of the taxe committee's mandate until 30 november 2015 as decided at the conference of presidents at the end of june in order for the taxe committee to fulfil its mandate-related tasks.
the european parliament, by decision of 12 february 2015, established the special committee on taxation and other measures similar in nature and effect on the basis of rule 197 of its rules of procedure. the article provides for the right to set up special committees whose powers, composition and duration of mandate are to be determined at the same time as the decision establishing them is taken. the committee was set up on a proposal from the conference of presidents and by a commission decision to examine the practice of tax rulings under eu state aid rules in all member states. it consists of 45 members, its term of office is six months from the date of adoption of that decision, and its primary objective is to shed light on the way in which member states tax in order to avoid unfair tax practices and to combat tax evasion in the european union. as i believe that this committee can contribute by its action to fair taxation practices within the member states of the european union and thus to the improvement and development of the economic image of the union itself, i supported the extension of its mandate. the existence of a special committee for tax rulings and other measures of a similar nature and effect is a logical way of achieving the eu's objectives and preventing activities that could jeopardise them.
