written. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution with the european parliament's recommendations to the commission on the negotiations on the transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip), as i believe that the partnership is good for the european and croatian economy. in the same way that for producers and exporters, eu accession has contributed to increasing the market and strengthening the attractiveness of croatia as a tourist destination, the transatlantic trade and investment partnership increases opportunities for croatian companies and improves opportunities for tourism. in addition, opportunities for foreign investment are increasing, which unfortunately are too few in croatia. i support ensuring, through these recommendations, a transparent ttip negotiation; leading to an ambitious, comprehensive and balanced trade and investment agreement of high standards; promoting sustainable growth with mutual benefits in the member states and mutual and reciprocal benefits for all partners; seeking the abolition of all customs tariffs; taking into account that visa facilitation for european service and goods providers is a crucial element; ensuring full recognition and strong legal protection of eu geographical indications and measures to deal with cases of misuse; continuing efforts to increase the transparency of negotiations by making more negotiation proposals available to the public.
written. ‒ the transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip) is of major geopolitical importance to both the european union and the united states. it will enhance bilateral relations between the world's two largest economies, but will also have an impact on the multilateral trading system. the aim is to promote economic growth, stimulate job creation and achieve better trading conditions. the commission notes that the ttip will have an impact on the republic of croatia, in particular on small and medium-sized enterprises. the reduction of unnecessary costs, simplification of administration and procedures, will make it much easier to place croatian products on the us market. the republic of croatia has a bilateral agreement with the united states dating back to 1996. however, ttip creates better conditions, i.e. a better framework for investment protection, which is why i supported this report.
written. ‒ the transatlantic trade and investment partnership is the most important eu-us project in recent times and the most significant trade agreement in the world currently being negotiated by eu-us negotiating teams. the political importance of this agreement is also invaluable for strengthening transatlantic cooperation in other areas. the european parliament, by adopting the resolution, supported the negotiations, but at the same time made clear its disagreements, fears and wishes to the eu negotiating team. i supported amendments which make it clear that it is necessary to accept that where the eu and the us have very different regulations there will be no agreement, particularly when it comes to public health services, genetically modified organisms, the use of hormones in the cattle sector, the reach regulation and its implementation and the cloning of animals for breeding, and that these issues cannot therefore be negotiated. the commission has also taken the view that the new rules on the protection of investors' interests should be based on the principle of the protection of legitimate expectations and the principle of the protection of legitimate expectations.
written. ‒ reducing regulatory barriers to trade is an important tool that ttip should help strengthen the european and us economies. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the measure is compatible with the internal market. the us is the eu's largest export market. the new agreement would open up new opportunities for eu companies to export to the us and encourage us companies to invest more in europe. studies show that the agreement could bring up to 100 billion euros a year to economies throughout latin america, africa, and asia, helping to combat poverty in developing countries. the impact of the agreement on smes, which are the main drivers of economic growth and development in the eu, is significant. the projections are that 6 out of 10 entrepreneurs will increase their earnings by 20 percent, and 4 out of 10 will employ more people. the comprehensive trade agreement should include a chapter on investor protection as security is one of the cornerstones of attracting investment. the european union has developed a number of mechanisms to involve citizens and interested public in public consultation processes that are also underpinned by serious analyses of how the proposed change will affect the economy, the environment and human rights, and i therefore support the report.
‒ ttip is an economic agreement that would mean greater economic growth and greater benefits for all countries. given that the eu is heavily dependent on trade and exports, its gdp would increase by 15 to 20 per cent by 2020. the european position would be enhanced and the world market would be more interconnected. the situation of smes would be considerably improved, and unnecessary costs, barriers and complicated procedures would be removed. the ttip creates the basis for the creation of the largest free trade area, resulting in economic growth in both the eu and the us, as well as the creation of new jobs. to make the conclusion of an agreement as prudent as possible, the eu is striving to have as transparent a negotiation as possible in order to correct any errors in a timely manner and to reach an agreement that is favourable to both parties. the key clause of ttip is the reduction of customs tariffs and the protection of workers and the environment. the us and the eu can really make a big step forward with this agreement. i am also aware that many eu citizens fear that this agreement could open the door to gmo food imports. however, the eu has spoken out and protected its citizens by making clear that it will not sacrifice its food safety, health and social standards, environment, data protection and cultural diversity standards.
written. ‒ i voted in favour of the recommendation on a draft council decision on the conclusion, on behalf of the european union and its member states, of the protocol to the stabilisation and association agreement between the european communities and their member states, of the one part, and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, of the other part, to take account of the accession of the republic of croatia to the european union, as the agreement is to be brought into line with the fact that the republic of croatia has become a member of the european union.
written. ‒ the stabilisation and association agreement is the newer version of the agreement for the candidate countries and governs the rules for the comprehensive cooperation of the european union and its member states with the candidate country. by signing the agreement, or more precisely the 'evolutionary clauses', a country becomes a potential member of the european union. the agreement covers the countries of south-east europe, and so far only the republic of croatia has become a full member. the main difference between the previous europe agreements and the stabilisation and association agreement is the greater emphasis on regional cooperation. in addition, the agreement governs a number of trade regulations, harmonisation of legislation, respect for rights and freedoms, financial regulations and many others. i support the report by mr ive vajgl, giving his consent to the signing of the protocol to take account of the accession of the republic of croatia to the european union, adding the republic of macedonia as a member to the stabilisation and association agreement and laying down the rules of cooperation between croatia and macedonia.
written. ‒ the stabilisation and association agreement between the european communities and their member states, on the one hand, and macedonia, on the other, is the first step that macedonia must take on its path towards the eu. the protocols, which govern the means of communication and the means of implementation of this agreement between its signatories, should be amended accordingly in view of the accession of the republic of croatia to the eu. i support this decision, as i support macedonia on its way to the eu. macedonia is fully prepared to start eu accession negotiations, much more prepared than other countries that want to join the eu, but also than some that are already eu members. i believe that the 10-year wait is demotivating for the macedonian people and does not contribute to the stability of the region. i therefore call on the european parliament, the european commission and the council to take a political decision to open negotiations with macedonia, as the decision to block the opening of negotiations is also purely political.

written. ‒ the greenhouse gas emissions trading system is an ambitious project that has not proved fully feasible in practice. it was established to meet the eu's emission reduction targets in a coordinated and cost-effective manner. however, at the beginning of the third trading period, the system was characterised by a large imbalance between supply and demand of allowances, leading to the creation of a surplus of around 2 billion allowances. this number is expected to increase over the coming years to more than 2,6 billion emission allowances by 2020. the impact assessment has shown that the establishment of a market security buffer could help to address the current imbalances and make the ets more resilient, and i therefore support this document.

written. ‒ growing inequality, poverty, racial and religious violence and hate crimes are some of the root causes of crime faced by the member states of the european union and therefore need to be further investigated. the commission therefore adopted on 24 april 2015 a communication entitled 'a european security agenda for 2015-2020', which replaces the internal security strategy (2010-2014). the new programme establishes priorities and guiding principles in the field of security, as well as union actions aimed at improving the exchange of information, strengthening operational cooperation and providing support measures to member states. i consider this type of document to be of great importance for the union itself, since freedom and security are fundamental rights of every eu citizen. this requires a coherent, comprehensive and harmonised eu deal that respects and ensures the fundamental rights of every human being. however, i abstained from voting on the resolution because it does not contain adequate answers and recommendations to key issues related to the fight against crime and the achievement of security in the area of financing, computer and organised crime and the fight against terrorism, which throughout the european union endangers the lives of its inhabitants.
written. ‒ threats to the union's internal security have become more complex, hybrid, asymmetrical and unconventional, and are present at international level, evolving rapidly and difficult to predict. as they are beyond the capabilities of each member state, they call more than ever for a coherent, comprehensive, multidimensional and coordinated eu response that takes full account of respect for fundamental rights. we need to strike a balance between preventive policies and repressive measures to preserve freedom, security and justice. the security measures must always be taken in accordance with the rule of law and the protection of fundamental rights such as the right to privacy and data protection, freedom of expression and association, and due process. the european union has not agreed on the definition of 'national security', thereby opening up an uncertain space for exceptions in eu legal instruments that mention 'national security', and i therefore join the calls on the commission to swiftly propose a definition of the national security exception in article 4 (2) teu and its limitation in order to ensure that security measures respect democratic principles and fundamental rights.
written. ‒ i support the motion for a resolution on the european agenda on security, as ensuring the security and freedom of european citizens is a shared responsibility of the union and the member states and a problem that requires full attention. in recent years, a number of threats have emerged in the eu's immediate neighbourhood, and i therefore agree that the eu urgently needs to assess security threats and focus on the four main priority areas listed in the resolution: terrorism, radicalisation, cybercrime and organised crime. this should be done by addressing the issue of security at the eu's borders, due to the threat of terrorism and radicalism, and by addressing the issue of cybercrime, as new technological developments often increase the impact of crime on citizens. the commission should also make further efforts to improve the exchange of information and operational cooperation between national intelligence and law enforcement services, with particular reference to organised crime, which is a major threat and the most serious threat to the security of eu citizens. in the light of all the above, i consider that this resolution is the best way to ensure that citizens' freedoms and security are protected in accordance with fundamental human rights.
‒ the european agenda on security 2015-2019 sets out challenges, principles and guidelines in dealing with security threats related to terrorism, extremism, organised crime and smuggling. the commission adopted the programme in april, and parliament, in the libe committee, failed to adopt the priorities in the commission's original proposal. instead, the amendments that were incorporated into the final resolution at the committee focused on human rights, data protection, and economic inequality as the root and crucial causes of crime. the amendments also followed the typical line of calling for greater union influence in the security policy segment, directly violating the principle of subsidiarity by insisting on the eu definition of national security and calling for the establishment of more forms of legal migration. that's why i voted against it.

written. ‒ as we live in a digital age characterised by rapid development and the need for control, there is a need for new modern copyright regulations that all stakeholders must be satisfied with. the right to private property is one of the fundamental human rights, therefore photographs, poems, video content and other creative constructs may not be used and published without the prior authorization of the author of the content. rapid development means that many aspects of the existing copyright regulations are not regulated, so there is still a great possibility of theft and piracy. furthermore, copyright protection is the basis for the high-quality functioning of the eu market and the development of this business segment as it represents a great potential and it is of great importance that every consumer is aware of all the elements of the content they use, and in particular whether they are using authorised or illegal content. i believe that it is necessary to harmonise certain aspects of copyright and related rights because it is of great importance to control the exchange and use of information, which is not easy given that we live in an accelerated information society. for these reasons, i have supported this resolution on the implementation of the directive on the harmonisation of certain aspects of copyright and related rights in the information society.

‒ the european endowment for democracy was established in 2012 with the aim of supporting political and civil society actors seeking to bring about democratic change in the eu's eastern and southern neighbourhoods. such support shall be achieved through the provision of rapid and flexible financial assistance tailored to the beneficiaries without any bureaucratic obstacles. the foundation's management and executive board shall be chaired by members of the european parliament. the committee shall be composed of representatives of the member states and of the eu institutions, including nine representatives of the european parliament. the european foundation for democracy shall act by providing support for the protection of human rights, democratic reforms, political participation and representation, which are the main tasks of the european instrument for democracy and human rights. the instrument is specifically designed to achieve the objectives set and it finances eu election observation projects, programmes and missions. the european instrument shall be used to award grants to civil society organisations, non-governmental organisations and human rights defenders. in addition to eradicating poverty, it also seeks to strengthen and sustain democracy in developing countries.

‒ the forced labour convention of 1930 is one of the founding conventions of the international labour organisation, which sets international labour standards and is considered a human rights instrument. it is still used in practice, but the international labour organization was concerned by information from the early 20th century that at least 20.9 million people were victims of forced labor. it is therefore necessary to adopt this protocol, which sets out measures to prevent forced labour in society as it constitutes a threat to fundamental human rights and an offence against human dignity. i believe that there is a need to educate and inform people and to make efforts to implement this protocol in order to eradicate forced labour to a large extent in the member states of the european union and beyond. people have the right to work and earn a living, but in a fair and dignified way, and any form of forced labour that violates human rights and dignity can be condemned. we should not create and support a society that is more akin to slavery than democracy, and therefore we need to eradicate all the risks that contribute to the survival of forced labour.

mr president, when the european commission declared 2013 the european year of citizens, it confirmed the democratic potential of the european parliament, the only directly elected body of the european union. it also recognises the importance of communication between citizens and institutions. a move away from the practice of simply letting the institutions' decisions be made public was announced, and citizens were put at the very centre of the european union's political agenda. it was therefore desirable to further strengthen the awareness of the citizens of the european union of their membership of the community, of their rights but also of their obligations, and of the influence they must retain on their daily lives. that is why citizens have taken the european citizens' initiative seriously. the european public has taken the opportunity to direct the commission with its million signatures to propose legislation within its remit, and today we decided on the first such democratic step. the human right to access to clean water is being defended today in the european parliament as is the right of the public to alert high politics to the vile passions of those who would turn the unique commodities of life - water, fertile soil, hydrocarbons - into increasingly scarce resources. i have supported and will continue to support such initiatives.

mr. president, i consider the right to water citizens' initiative to be extremely important not because it is the first citizen initiative of its kind, but because it draws attention to water as a public good, but also to water as a human right. it is the duty of the member states to protect water sources from privatisation and pollution. and also make sure that water, drinking water, is available to all of our citizens. i think that this initiative has succeeded in reaching those basic segments that i have advocated in my personal and political life, and i have therefore supported this report. i also think it is important that it is recognised that special attention should be given to low-income populations, to those living in rural areas and to underdeveloped regions. water must not be allowed to become a source of wealth or illegal profit for state or private service providers. there is an urgent need to address water pollution and to provide citizens with an insight into water quality. from an environmental perspective, good water management will become a priority in the coming decades, as water is important for economic development, energy stability and agricultural production, and without water there is no life.
‒ the commission published an official response in april 2014 that only partially met the requests of the initiators and signatories of the initiative. the commission agreed that water management should, as a rule, be the responsibility of the local authorities closest to the citizens, that water is not a marketable product and that water and sanitation should be excluded from the concession directive. while these are positive steps, the commission has avoided committing to propose legislation that would label access to drinking water as a human right and has not given guarantees that the right to water and related services will be protected from further liberalisation and trade agreements such as ttip. i therefore support this report and hope that the commission's handling of this citizens' initiative will not diminish the potential of this tool of eu democracy.

written. ‒ right2water is the first and most successful european citizens' initiative, and a great example of participatory democracy. the initiative, under the slogans 'water is a public good, not a commodity' and 'water and sanitation are a human right', has achieved 1.6 million verified signatures from all member states, a major achievement. i think it is necessary to recall the central objectives of the initiative, which is that the eu institutions and the member states have a duty to ensure that all residents have the right to water and sanitation. water supply and management should not be subject to market rules, water services must be excluded from liberalisation and the eu should step up its efforts to achieve universal access to water. unfortunately, despite the initiative's request, the commission did not give guarantees to prevent further liberalisation of water and sanitation services and exclusion of water from trade agreements, which disappointed the initiative's organisers. on the other hand, i would welcome the commission's start to recognise and accept public-private partnerships. the commission has also examined the possibility of a public-private partnership between the public utilities and the private sector in the member states.

member of the commission.– mr president, firstly, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, ms vozemberg, and the committee on women’s rights and gender equality (femm committee) for this initiative. the draft report on women’s careers in science and university and the glass ceilings encountered is a very welcome move. it reflects well the current state of play and proposes concrete ideas to move forward. let me share with you a few thoughts on it. first: institutional changes. as was rightly mentioned in the report, these are very much needed to remove institutional barriers and bias. in science, men and women may have the same qualifications, but they often do not have the same chances to succeed because of persisting discrimination and stereotypes concerning the role and capacities of women. there are still practices and attitudes that produce inequalities. institutional changes can help on the way towards assuring that research institutions guarantee equal opportunities for both women and men at all levels. to this end, in the european research area, research institutions are encouraged to adopt fully—fledged gender equality plans which include a detailed account of the state of play on gender equality within the organisation, measures to address existing bias, setting targets and monitoring of progress. with institutional changes we have moved on from women-focused programmes, which are useful initiatives but are not necessarily sustainable in the long run. institutional changes in research organisations are today the cornerstone of the commission’s strategy on gender equality in research. in horizon 2020, our framework programme for research and innovation, these institutional changes are clearly pursued, but we need to do more and we need to do better. we need all member states to engage in the same line in the context of the european research area. i am glad that the european parliament is on board as its help and its role is crucial. second: the importance of enforcing the existing regulatory framework on gender equality. this is stated at the outset of the report, and the commission fully agrees. it is not enough to have laws; we need effective implementation and enforcement. the commission monitors the correct application by member states of existing eu legislation on gender equality. in research, we also need to address the specificities of the sector with concrete actions, both at the eu and national level. in may 2015, the council adopted the european research area roadmap and called on the member states and the commission to implement top action priorities through action plans and strategies. translating national equality legislation into effective action is one key priority. the roadmap also states that gaps in cross-cutting gender equality legislation at eu and national levels should be addressed. we know that national laws, strategies and incentives have a positive impact in triggering actions by research institutions. this is important, as research institutions are the ones ultimately responsible for implementing institutional changes through gender equality plans. the council asked for appropriate indicators to monitor the progress made at national and eu level, as does the european parliament in its report. again, the commission fully agrees. the ‘she figures 2015’ leaflet was published last july, and a full report will be published in january 2016. in this endeavour, the commission would like to underline the need for a full collaboration from the member states in order to produce robust indicators. third: gender balance in decision making in research bodies and institutions. participation of women in decision making is just as important. women are still under-represented in decision making and the phenomenon is not self-correcting. in response to this, we see that many european states are choosing to set targets or quotas. in 2013, 18 states did so, compared to just 8 in 2008. there is a need to clearly call for improvement on the gender balance in decision making. before concluding, i would like to mention three important initiatives on gender equality. the first is on work-life balance. the commission has just published, in early august, a roadmap in preparation of a broad initiative to improve work-life balance and a decision for 2016. the commission will consider a mix of legislative and non-legislative instruments including a modern solution to the needs of today’s families. we will now start the consultation process. the european parliament, the member states and the social partners will have a very important role to play in this process. the second is the 2012 commission proposal for improving gender balance on boards of listed companies. the proposal is currently supported by a majority of member states, and once adopted by the parliament and the council it will pave the way for further progress on gender equality. thirdly, we also share members’ concerns on the gender pay gap, which at eu level persists at 16.4%. last year, the commission adopted a recommendation on pay transparency aiming to assist member states and other stakeholders in a more effective application of existing equal pay legislation. it provides a toolkit of concrete measures to tackle pay inequality and the gender pay gap. we look forward to receiving, by the end of this year, member states’ notifications on the national measures taken in accordance with the recommendation. we will then assess the need for possible further measures. in conclusion, both women and men are needed if europe is to achieve its ambitions in r&i for the benefit of the whole of society. the commission will continue to do its part, but to achieve gender equality the commitment of the european parliament in terms of the policy and financial engagement of the member states remains essential. the commission will take good note of all the recommendations made in the report.

the budapest convention on the contract for the carriage of goods by inland waterways entered into force on 1 april 2015. it covers issues such as the rights and obligations of the parties to the contract, transport documents, the liability of drivers and the time limits for making claims. the convention applies to contracts for the international carriage of goods between states at least one of which is a party to the convention and contributes to the internal market in transport, the harmonisation of contracts and internal navigation standards throughout europe. the convention is an agreement falling within the exclusive competence of the european union. however, it does not allow the union to become a party, but member states cannot ratify or accede to the convention without the approval of the union. eleven member states are already parties to the convention and 15 have indicated that they do not have inland waterways covered by this convention. austria and poland have expressed an interest in acceding to the convention. belgium ratified the convention on 5 august 2008, after the entry into force of the rome regulation. i supported the report authorising belgium and poland to ratify and austria to accede to the convention, because the implementation of this legal instrument has broad implications for the development of transport rights as well as for the development of small and medium-sized enterprises in the vicinity of inland waterways.
‒ the budapest convention on the contract for the carriage of goods by inland waterways, which entered into force on 1 april 2005, contributes to the internal market in transport by harmonising contractual and internal navigation standards across europe. the convention does not provide for the possibility of the european union becoming a party. however, member states cannot ratify or accede to the convention without the approval of the european union. the eleven member states of the european union with inland waterways covered by the convention have already become parties to it and benefit from the benefits it offers them, and the eu recognises the importance of signing the convention for its member states. recognising the importance of the creation of instruments for the harmonisation of contractual and internal navigational standards throughout europe and the benefits they bring to the signatory countries, i support the granting of ratification of the budapest convention to the kingdom of belgium and the republic of poland and the accession of the republic of austria to the convention.

madam president, during the war in croatia, i had the opportunity to help many of the displaced and refugees from bosnia and herzegovina and to feel what it means to be homeless, to be left without everything. that is why i am supporting today what the commission is doing, the actions and the positions we have and condemning what happened on monday. however, i want to warn you that the migrant crisis has practically shifted to croatia. in the last 24 hours, refugees have been coming into croatia, and what's important is that the croatian government has shown seriousness at this point, but croatia cannot solve this problem on its own. and that is why it is important that the commission immediately help our country so that croatia can cope with the wave of refugees that will surely follow. in addition, i must say, we have a great example from kutina where young people are even preparing a cultural program for refugees. such people need support, but the commission and the european union must act and show solidarity in action.
madam president, as we are having this debate, the first hundred refugees are entering croatia. all around our country, borders are being closed, walls are being erected and railways are being blocked, so it's unclear at this point whether anyone will want to take in the surplus of refugees that croatia has nothing to offer. clearly, fences, walls and roadblocks are not the answer, but they are not the product of someone's madness. part of the responsibility certainly lies with brussels, which has sent messages that clearly do not have the support of all member states. today, the large numbers of people in the refugee camp have nothing to do with the wars in syria and iraq. they come from countries not directly affected by conflict, and they come because european officials have told them that europe has room for everyone. europe should have a place for women, children, the elderly and those facing certain death if they remain in their homeland, and for economic migrants, this europe of concern should have had a common immigration policy long ago.
written. more than 100,000 people are waiting for our answer whether we will approve or reject the commission's proposal and receive them. i support the commission's proposal because it is realistic and guarantees the dignity of all those fleeing the war in syria. it is a proposal that will enable us to show solidarity with those in need and to build the europe we believe in. i support the quota system, but i think it's a temporary solution. it is necessary to address the causes of these people leaving their countries and to see what the eu is doing to root out the causes, to stabilise the situation and to keep migration under control, because security reports say that among the refugees there are those who have bought syrian passports and who could potentially pose a security threat. we need a common comprehensive strategy involving all countries and all parties, which will contribute to the protection of our external borders, but also to the protection of those fleeing war. this is not just a humanitarian issue, but also a security, economic and social issue, and we must be prepared to provide these people with dignity, while ensuring that eu citizens live in safety and preserving our internal stability.
president of the council. madam president, it would be easy to move on to another item on the agenda. but it so happens that this item on the agenda, which we are now going to deal with, is not unrelated to the one we have just discussed. the debate has, of course, focused on refugees, who are the victims of conflicts, of terrible wars that tear apart a number of countries. but a number of members have noted that among these refugees there are of course also people who are called refugees or economic migrants, as if the poverty, as if the absolute destitution they often face were not a reason to go looking for a better life elsewhere. what about the young people in africa and elsewhere who have no prospect of finding a job, no prospect of a decent life? in the end, are these young people not right to leave, to set off too? we are talking, of course, about economic migrants, migrants who would have fewer rights. yes, perhaps they have no rights under the geneva convention, but is not absolute poverty a reason to leave and seek a little better life elsewhere? so i would like to repeat a little what president juncker said last week: who are we europeans to condemn these millions of people who want to go elsewhere? not so long ago - because in history, a century or a century and a half is a relatively short period of time - millions of europeans set out because they were poor, because they had no economic and social prospects in europe, because they had nothing to offer their children. they went looking for a better life elsewhere and looked in particular to the new world that had welcomed them. therefore, we must understand. it should be noted that one third of the luxembourg population - and i believe there are other countries in similar situations - left for the united states because they could not survive in luxembourg. so poverty affects us. and the poverty that is elsewhere concerns us. this is the reality of a globalized world. migration is part of this globalized world, and especially in a globalized world where, at the end of the day, even those who live in the back of africa have information, means of communication, means of getting an idea of what their life could be like if they could live it elsewhere. this debate therefore concerns us and, in a certain sense, it is a continuation of the previous debate because the answer, here too, to these so-called economic migrants cannot be the construction of new walls, the construction of new barbed wire or the use of tear gas, for the moment, we do not know what will happen next. the answer to this problem is development. it's a global economy that doesn't condemn millions, if not billions, of human beings to total destitution, not to mention climate refugees, refugees who are already the victims, today, of climate problems and global warming. that is why the adoption of the 2030 agenda for sustainable development is so important and must be a top priority for europe, because here too we are in the front line if we fail to combat poverty effectively in our neighbours, in our african neighbours and elsewhere. following the work of the addis ababa conference on financing for development, the sustainable development summit in new york is the second major milestone of this year 2015, which should hopefully - i believe that hopes are justified - conclude with the adoption of a universal climate agreement in december in paris at cop 21. the final outcome of the post-2015 process can be considered as overall satisfactory. indeed, the european union's main objective of adopting an ambitious, transformative and sustainable sustainable development agenda has been more or less achieved. we are still waiting for final adoption by the summit at the end of this month in new york. the agenda includes a set of objectives that integrate in a balanced way the three dimensions of sustainable development and pursue a primary objective: poverty eradication. in this context, we can welcome the fact that the action programme resulting from the addis ababa conference on financing for development is the cornerstone of the means of implementing the 2030 agenda and includes both financial and non-financial means to implement the future development agenda. i would like to underline the role of parliament in this collective success and thank you for your support throughout the negotiation process. in this context, i would like to mention in particular the work of mr stier on your november 2014 resolution on the comprehensive development framework beyond 2015 and that of ms theocharous on the role of local authorities in development cooperation. we must now take action, that is, implement the 2030 agenda. to do this, we must first examine all the instruments at our disposal and determine whether they are adequate. the programme represents a significant development in relation to the millennium development goals, particularly in its universal character which means that it will have to be implemented by all and at all levels of development. it is not just for developing countries, it is an agenda for sustainable development. we get back to this idea that we all live on the same planet and that there are no rich people on one side and those who unfortunately don't have the chance to be rich people on the other. in this context, the commission will have to examine all european legislation in the various sectors concerned and, if necessary, present appropriate legislative proposals to the european parliament and the council. member states will also need to review their sustainable development strategies and instruments in the light of the 2030 agenda. the implementation and monitoring of the 2030 agenda is not only a matter for governments and administrations but for all actors, including civil society and the private sector. the programme incorporates a robust monitoring and control mechanism which was one of the major difficulties during the negotiations. we now have a framework to assess progress and report back to the citizens. in implementing the 2030 agenda, we also need to ensure that the balance between the three dimensions of sustainable development - economic, social and environmental - is maintained, and i count on the support of parliament. on the council side, the ministers for development and environment will have the opportunity to discuss the continuation of the process and the coordination of the process on 26 october in luxembourg. there are also strong links between the 2030 agenda for sustainable development and the cop 21 conference, which will take place in paris from 30 november to 11 december. for the luxembourg presidency, it will be crucial to ensure that we build on the progress made in addis ababa and new york to ensure that the paris conference is also a success. with regard to this paris conference, reconciling development and climate action is possible, but it is not only possible, it is absolutely essential. this is why the 2030 agenda for sustainable development has created a new objective: urgent action to combat climate change and its consequences. this objective calls for an ambitious and universal agreement in december in paris at cop 21. preparing for cop 21 is one of the main priorities of our presidency and this friday the environment and finance ministers will be discussing climate finance at their meeting. the environment council will adopt conclusions as early as friday which will serve as a mandate for cop 21. the position of the european union and its member states is clear. the 2015 agreement should, firstly, be a universal and legally binding agreement to effectively combat climate change and to contain the increase in the average global temperature to at least two degrees below pre-industrial levels. second, a deal that is made to last, that offers a long-term vision of the transformation needed towards resilient, low-carbon societies and economies that are able to withstand the effects of climate change. thirdly, a flexible agreement with the capacity to respond dynamically to changing scientific and technological knowledge, responsibilities and capacities and to allow for broad and effective participation. finally, an agreement with mechanisms to measure progress and deepen ambition. we need a sound, rules-based regime, including rules on monitoring, verification of emissions and clear compatibility of emissions for all countries. the parties' actions will need to be irreversible and to move towards low carbon emissions. an agreement with a long-term objective, which should send a strong signal for transforming the development trajectories of countries to become low-carbon economies that are resilient to the effects of climate change. i would add that funding will be an important element, with a public and private commitment at the heart of the scheme of $100 billion a year by 2020 from developed countries to the poorest and most vulnerable countries, and more broadly, a re-direction of investment towards low-carbon and economically viable technologies. this is a great prospect for rebooting our economies and making a real technological leap and supporting sustainable growth. finally, i would like to stress that we welcome the support, here too, of the european parliament and its rapporteur, mr gilles pargneaux, to help us reach an agreement in paris in the near future.
first vice-president of the commission.– madam president, i will make some specific comments on development—related elements for the summit on sustainable development and cop 21, but before doing this, i want to make a more general remark. it is almost a year ago that, in the course of the hearings in this parliament, president juncker decided to hand me responsibility for sustainable development in a broad sense to create coherence in our policies. i want to point to the fact that one of the factors that will determine whether we will be successful with these policies is whether we are able to create coherence between the different elements – and we lack coherence. we lack coherence in my institution, we lack coherence in this institution, in the council, in the member states, in the international world. i think my first plea to you today would be, let us work together to create coherence between the actions of the dgs in the commission, the different committees in the european parliament. let us face it, sometimes the policies that come out of different dgs and different committees have contradictions. that is a reality, so let us try and do away with contradictions. i am at your disposal, i say to the members of this parliament, to do better than we have done up till now. i really want to make sure that we are coherent, because sustainable development has three main aspects: obviously environmental; but also economic, and social. these elements have a role inside the european union, and obviously worldwide, and as long as we are not able to create coherence between these different dimensions our approach will not be successful enough and will, if it continues to be contradictory, also lead to a waste of financial resources, human resources, political resources. the adoption of the 2030 agenda for sustainable development is going to be a landmark achievement, i think, because it has an inclusive nature already. it is something the european union has been advocating for a long time and i think this time, for once, citizens, parliaments, civil society, made the contributions, not just governments, and the way this parliament was involved in the process testifies to that different approach. the european union had an instrumental role in shaping the agenda; a lot will be expected of the european union also in new york, and president juncker has asked me to lead the delegation. there are 17 sustainable development goals which follow and expand on the mdgs. as i said, they would have to integrate economic, social and environmental dimensions, as well as human rights, gender equality, the rule of law, good governance and peaceful and inclusive societies. let me come back to this point because i think it is crucial. a holistic approach is what we need, but there is always a big danger in a holistic approach. if you say you need to do everything you end up doing nothing. but if you only leave the different silos on their own you might achieve something in one silo, nothing in another, etc. so the challenge here is to be precise on the specific issues without ever forgetting that you need to integrate it with other policies. parliaments will have to have an important role to play in that, and governments as well, but civil society should never be forgotten, because integrating policies is actually better done mostly in civil society than at governmental level. we have agreed a global partnership, it is ambitious, and i think we are determined to change, to integrate our internal and external policies, preparing for the special world bank and imf meeting in lima in october. second, we are preparing to launch specific new climate-relevant initiatives, including a new phase of the global climate change alliance with a budget of at least eur 350 million that will support adaptation to climate in vulnerable countries, notably least-developed countries and small island developing states. it will vice-president of the commission.– madam president, on behalf of the commission, i would like to thank parliament for supporting the proposal to amend the common provisions regulation as regards specific measures for greece. the proposal is an exceptional measure to address the unique situation in greece. the commission’s proposal follows the agreement reached in july at the euro summit. the agreement reached between co-legislators to maintain the commission proposal – and the exceptional speed which with which they processed this – is a concrete sign of european solidarity. the proposal must be seen in the wider context of the reform process undertaken by greece. timely and effective implementation of reforms to modernise the state and the economy, as agreed under the third programme, is crucial to ensure financial stability, fiscal sustainability and sound economic fundamentals for investment, job creation and growth. it is crucial to dispel any uncertainty and ensure a sound financial sector. with capital controls in place, the financing streams of the real economy are strained at a time when investment is needed most. the eu funds have an important role in this respect. there are substantial means available from the eu budget for greece but the implementation of the project, co-financed with eu funds, is held back by the tight liquidity situation of the greek state. to help address this situation we have put forward three exceptional measures so that the investment supported by eu funds can take place, and take place swiftly. for the 2014-2020 period, it is proposed to increase the rate of initial pre—financing for greece by seven percentage points for the european regional development fund, the cohesion fund, the european social fund and the european maritime and fisheries fund. this frontloading should allow for starting more investments earlier. for the 2007-2013 period, two measures are proposed: firstly to release the last five percent of the remaining eu payments, which are normally retained until the closure of the programmes in 2017 and, secondly, to remove the obligation to provide for national cofinancing and to apply the 100% eu financing rate. these measures should help bring the investment finance for the 2007-2013 period to a successful conclusion. all these measures would translate into eur 2 billion available for greece over the two years 2015 and 2016. importantly, these measures are budget-neutral for the current multiannual financial framework and would have no impact on the payment plan either. the additional pre-financing for the 2014-2020 programmes should be covered by payment application by the end of 2016. it is, of course, crucial to ensure that the money duly reaches the beneficiaries and does so as quickly as possible in line with the rules of sound financial management. to this end, a ring-fencing mechanism will ensure that additional amounts for the 2007-2013 period are used only for payments to beneficiaries. greece has already put such a mechanism in place. moreover, greece is required to report on the implementation of these measures by the end of 2016 and in the final implementation report for the 2007-2013 period. the commission has stood by greece throughout the crisis with both financial support and technical assistance. we will continue to support greece, both in the implementation of the reforms and in making the best use of eu funds. technical assistance is already being provided through the new structural reform support service which is available to all eu member states. technical meetings and ad hoc missions on the ground are being organised. as it happens, commissioner crețu is in greece today. i am looking forward to your debate.
the commission has also taken note of the fact that the greek authorities have not yet provided the commission with a full explanation of the reasons for the delay in the adoption of the measures. greece must implement reforms that the tsipras government has been running away from in the last term, and voters recently rewarded it for such behavior. i believe therefore that in the coming period there will be no significant improvement in the implementation of structural reforms, which makes our efforts to help greece a bit futile. the commission notes that the greek authorities have not provided any evidence that the restructuring plan is in line with the restructuring plan. i believe that to be true, but i must express my disagreement with such a strategy. increasing government spending is certainly not going to get the country out of the crisis because it's such irresponsible behavior that got it into it. for our efforts to make any sense, the new greek government must attract private investors and strengthen the private sector at the expense of the public. is the tsipras government ready for that? what measures does it plan to take to achieve this? i fear that in the long run, these moves are not helping our friends and partners in greece, but pushing them deeper into the abyss. if greece had not been a member of the eurozone, which it was admitted to under questionable circumstances, it would have been much harder to get into debt all these years and would be in much less trouble today. we may have stopped giving the greeks unconditional gifts of european taxpayers' money, but we continue to encourage them to overspend with formulations like this that public investment sets as a prerequisite for sustainable recovery. the commission notes that the greek authorities have not provided any evidence that the restructuring plan is in line with the restructuring plan. everything else is a mere livelihood that both the greeks and the european taxpayers are tired of.

member of the commission.– madam president, as this assembly knows, policy is local and, as with any other policy, development cooperation policy also has to be local. that is why i would like to thank parliament for its resolution on the role of local authorities in development cooperation. it highlights a common belief that the roots of democracy and well-being are local. development starts at the local level. most jobs, basic social services, political and civic rights are provided first and foremost in cities or regions or through local branches of government. moreover, i agree with the resolution where it states that, in order to be adequate and legitimate, policies have to be defined through a bottom-up approach. this means that they have to start with local authorities. i am convinced that the newly adopted 2030 agenda for sustainable development can only be of benefit if all actors are involved and mobilised. to that end, all public and private representatives, including local authorities, have to be involved in the implementation of the sustainable development goals. the world’s urban population will reach 70% by 2050. having a specific goal dedicated to urbanisation is therefore of crucial importance. but beyond the specific sustainable development goal, cities will be the frontline of all other issues, including migration, environmental sustainability, climate resilience, fragility and inequalities. local authorities will need human, institutional and financial resources to fulfil their missions. the transfer of financial resources from central governments remains a difficult aspect of decentralisation, and it is often overlooked. all these issues are a question of sovereignty. we will address this through our political dialogue with partner countries, with the objective of ensuring coherent and efficient implementation. since 2013, the commission has been working on empowering local authorities in partner countries for enhanced governance and more effective development outcomes. this work will now be intensified. we have started to deliver on this commitment following four priorities, which are: supporting decentralisation reforms and local initiatives; strengthening the capacity of local authorities; addressing the challenges brought to the fore by rapid urbanisation; and engaging with associations of local authorities at all levels. these priorities are all covered by the resolution to be adopted in parliament. as an example of our cooperation, in january this year the commission signed the first framework partnership agreements with five global and regional associations of local authorities. these agreements formalise our reinforced support. we are also backing up our political commitment by providing adequate resources: eur 450 million has already been secured from the dedicated programme of the instrument for development cooperation on civil society organisations and local authorities. all eu instruments are gradually taking local governments into account as well. approximately eur 1.7 billion will be used to support decentralisation reforms, rural development and local governance in the period up to 2020. these precious resources must be used to ensure delivery and concrete results in empowering local authorities in the implementation of development cooperation.

‒ the forced labour convention is one of the eight core conventions of the international labour organisation (ilo) that defines international labour standards and is considered an instrument for ensuring human rights. the protocol requires ilo member states to adopt national policies and action plans for the effective and equitable abolition of forced labour and creates measures to implement the provisions of the protocol. it also sets out measures that ilo member states must implement to prevent forced labour by educating and informing people and by applying legislation to prevent forced labour and protect people from potentially fraudulent employment. the protocol provides for certain measures for the identification, release, protection, recovery and rehabilitation of victims, together with other forms of assistance and support. i supported the report of representative stevens approving the protocol because i believe that forced labor is against fundamental human rights. ratification of the protocol is necessary to make progress in preventing trafficking in human beings, labour exploitation and the protection and compensation of victims of forced labour.
written. ‒ the original convention on forced labour entered into force almost 100 years ago, but forced labour still affects some 21 million people worldwide. contrary to popular belief, the european union is not exempt from forced labor, with a rate of 7 percent of people working against their will. cases of forced domestic workers or agricultural workers have been found in all eu countries. not only is forced labor a violation of basic human rights but it also generates illegal profits of at least $150 billion a year, according to a report by the international labor organization. thus, it is a crime that affects not only the individual but also society and the world economy. the ratification of the 2014 protocol is an important step in the fight against forced labour worldwide and in the european union, as well as an important step in the fight against crimes closely related to forced labour, such as trafficking in human beings, prostitution and child pornography. i therefore welcome and have supported the recommendation on a draft council decision authorising member states to ratify, in the interest of the european union, the protocol on matters within the european union's competence relating to judicial cooperation in criminal matters.

written. ‒ what is the value of european skills, traditions and knowledge? if it's done in small quantities, it's expensive. and it very easily disappears under the onslaught of counterfeits from third countries. for example, european textile manufacturers complain that about 40 percent of their revenue is spent on litigating counterfeiters instead of increasing production, and many factories have long since closed. a designation of origin has many advantages that a protected designation of origin does not have. above all, it is consumer recognition. consumers like to buy products with a genuine label because they know they are buying quality and authenticity. instead, when they get home, they turn over the overpriced product and it says "made in china". small craftsmen and poor regions would benefit most from such a label. four million new jobs! the legal basis has already been laid with the labelling of agricultural products, and the new copyright directive is already the first stop on which we can start building a success story immediately. when someone skeptical talks to me about this subject, i simply ask them where european agriculture would be if there were no origin labels for, say, wines, or certain fruit or meat products? we must not be afraid to protect what is ours and ask our trading partners to respect it!

written. ‒ i support the report on the possible extension of the european union's geographical indication to non-agricultural products. the eu has a unique gi protection system for agricultural products, which is based on the principle of 'one country, two systems'. the extension of the protection of geographical indications to non-agricultural products will have multiple positive effects. for consumers, it will mean providing reliable information on the place and method of production of a particular product. in addition, the extension of protection will contribute to the sustainability of the operations of small and medium-sized enterprises, which are the backbone of the european union's economy and employ some 33 million people. manufacturers across the european union have been building quality policies for their products for years. the designation of origin is one of the main factors that gives them a competitive advantage, contributes significantly to the preservation of their cultural and gastronomic traditions and supports rural development together with market support measures and producer income. those companies often lack sufficient financial means to protect their products and therefore need protection at union level to ensure the promotion of high quality eu products, both on the internal market and on the global market.

written. ‒ being closer to citizens than any other public institution, local authorities have the most important responsibility for the welfare of the local population. the role of local actors is essential in the creation of any successful policy, as such stakeholders are responsible for regional development and strengthening social cohesion. the importance of local actors stems from their adaptation to the context, as well as their knowledge of the challenges, needs, problems and concerns of the local population. such challenges include social exclusion, migration, food security, resource depletion, public security and violence, climate adaptation, rule of law, access to justice and more. however, in order to strengthen the role of local authorities in promoting cooperation with developing countries, it is first necessary to ensure the fairest possible transfer of financial resources from the national (and even european) to the local level, i.e. to the level of cities and municipalities. the quality of local government is primarily linked to the political readiness of the central government to ensure the implementation of decisions at the local level, through legal and regulatory instruments, allowing local authorities to use a sufficient degree of autonomy in exercising power and acquiring certain capabilities. it is precisely because of the indispensable role of local actors in the development of sustainable cooperation and their close links with the local population that i support this report.
written. ‒ the subsidiarity principle is one of the european union's founding principles, which guarantees and demonstrates a commitment to tackling issues and problems at the level at which they arise, which is particularly relevant in the context of the local community's needs, i.e. their role in driving development, which this proposal addresses. in this regard, the proposal's emphasis on strengthening the capacity of local authorities to achieve the integration of the social, economic and environmental dimensions of development is particularly important and commendable. strengthening local authorities implies efforts to develop sustainable and institutionalised forms of cooperation and communication between all levels of government within the eu, but also horizontally with other stakeholders such as civil society organisations and the private sector. in this context, it is necessary to support the proposal's efforts to strengthen the involvement of local authorities as full-fledged actors in the implementation of the european development fund, i.e. to ensure a genuinely participatory process.
written. ‒ good governance at local level is essential to achieving sustainable development. i support the report by mrs theocharous, who welcomes the support for strengthening the capacity of local authorities and the structure for their coordination at national, regional and european level. it is necessary to encourage partnerships between local authorities in member states and developing countries to achieve greater good, such as better planning for environmental protection. the quality of local government is primarily linked to the political willingness of central government to give a sufficient degree of autonomy to local authorities through legal and regulatory instruments. by achieving a degree of autonomy, local authorities can manage and implement public policies and services on the basis of local political decision-making processes and interaction with other public institutions, as well as with citizens and the private sector. coordination and policy dialogue with local authorities are necessary to allow the evaluation of results achieved, the identification of obstacles and the identification of opportunities to improve impacts at local level. in this context, i would also stress the need to allocate additional resources to strengthen the capacity of local authorities to provide better quality public services, guarantee equal opportunities and social cohesion.
written. ‒ i support this report because local authorities, as key state and institutional actors for governance at local level, will have a key role to play in achieving the post-2015 objectives. increasing democratic decision-making at local level and sustainable territorial development based on the participation of the local community will lead to the empowerment of local authorities. they also represent a strong link between the community and national and global goals for the coming period. the eu is also heavily involved in supporting local authorities in developing countries to reduce poverty and achieve the millennium development goals. the rio declaration emphasises the key role of indigenous peoples and their communities in development and environmental management. climate change and environmental degradation threaten poverty reduction and pose a major challenge to local governments. the eu and its member states should therefore remain the main driver of local government development and the most important provider of official development assistance.
written. ‒ given that they are closer to the local population than some other public institutions, local authorities are responsible for mobilising and implementing the views of local societies. this responsibility concerns in particular effective public administration, a greater number of large-scale development processes in cooperation with civil society organisations, and finding solutions to urgent challenges faced by local communities, such as social isolation, migration, food security, rapid urbanisation, public safety and the environmental impact of extractive activities. the quality of local government governance is primarily linked to the central government's willingness to create an environment in which the local government will acquire certain capabilities and effectively implement them in its own area. it is therefore necessary to emphasise that the quality of local governance depends largely on the way local authorities implement the necessary laws and services at local level, and how they cooperate with other public institutions, citizens and the private sector. i support this view because good governance at the local level is necessary to achieve sustainable development and ensure fair outcomes.

written. ‒ the commission's proposals for amendments to the european small claims procedure have been well received, given the particular shortcomings and untapped potential of the existing regulation. the commission correctly estimates that raising the threshold for accelerated procedures to eur 10 000 could resolve as many as half of cross-border business lawsuits in the eu, instead of the current 20%. the commission should also be able to take into account the need to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods and services are applied in a uniform manner throughout the union. i support the rapporteur's proposal for a three-year period after the entry into force of the regulation, during which member states would have the time and opportunity to provide such infrastructure. i also support the proposal that each member state be obliged to provide only one means of distance payment of its choice and that each member state determine independently the threshold of minimum income below which a party is not obliged to pay court fees. i consider that these proposals improve the technological and legal level of implementation without interfering with existing national legislation of the member states. the commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 290 tfeu concerning the establishment of a european data protection supervisor, the appointment of a european data protection supervisor and the appointment of a european data protection supervisor.
written. ‒ the establishment of the european small claims procedure should simplify and speed up litigation on small claims in cross-border cases and reduce costs. the procedure is established and specifically designed to help consumers and small and medium-sized enterprises (smes) to enforce their claims, thereby ensuring access to justice. it has also proven to be a useful tool, reducing the cost of cross-border small claims by up to 40% and the duration of the case from two years and five months to an average of five months. parliament stated in its resolution of 25 october 2011 that 'the use of small claims courts in some member states is significantly lower and that more needs to be done in terms of legal certainty, language barriers and transparency of proceedings'. the simplified procedure is also available for cross-border claims between eur 2 000 and eur 10 000 and an increased proportion of cases qualify for a significant reduction in costs and the length of litigation. it is therefore of the utmost importance to facilitate access to the necessary information for potential users, in particular consumers. i support the rapporteur on raising the threshold for using the european small claims procedure.
written. ‒ the european small claims procedure is an important instrument for citizens and businesses as it improves access to justice by simplifying court proceedings for cross-border small claims in civil and commercial disputes and reducing costs. it was established by regulation (ec) no 861/2007 and applies from 1 january 2009. the agreement applies when at least one of the parties is resident or habitually resident in a member state other than that of the court seised. at the parliamentary sitting i voted in favour of amending several elements of regulation (ec) no 861/2007. the main elements are: increasing the threshold for small claims from eur 2 000 to eur 5 000, an obligation for member states to ensure that the court fees are proportionate and do not exceed the court fees charged for national simplified court procedures, and linking the european small claims procedure and the european payment order procedure by allowing the claimant to use the european small claims procedure when a challenge to a european payment order has been lodged.
written. ‒ i support this report because consumers should be able to take full advantage of the opportunities offered by the single market and therefore their confidence should not be limited by the lack of effective legal solutions to disputes with a cross-border element. improving the european small claims procedure offers consumers an effective remedy and thus contributes to the exercise of their rights in practice. the commission should be able to take into account the fact that the legal basis for the application of the contested decision is the case law of the member state concerned. the commission should also be able to use the information provided by the member states to assess the effectiveness of the union's financial instruments. the european small claims procedure will also benefit from technological developments in the field of justice that can eliminate geographical distances and their consequences, which are the cause of high costs and lengthy procedures as a factor discouraging access to justice.
written. regulation (ec) no 861/2007 of 11 july 2007 establishing a european small claims procedure aims to simplify and speed up the litigation process in respect of cross-border small claims and to reduce costs. the regulation is designed solely as a means of helping consumers and smes to manage their disputes by ensuring access to justice. while the process has proven to be extremely useful, there is plenty of room for further expansion and development. the european small claims procedure has reduced the cost of litigation in cross-border small claims cases by up to 40%, and the duration of litigation from two years and five months to an average of five months. however, it should be noted that the rate of use of such courts for small claims in some member states is still very low and much more needs to be done in terms of legal certainty, the use of modern technology and the transparency of judicial proceedings. it is precisely because of the success of this procedure in the past in terms of reducing costs and the duration of the litigation itself that i fully support this report.

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam president, i have to confess to you that i too am a feminist because i had the opportunity to work in development cooperation in a previous life. i have gained the absolute conviction that development comes through women, it comes through women's education and it comes through women's integration into economic life. i really believe that the future of development is women. equality between men and women is at the heart of european values. it is an integral part of the legal and political framework of the european union. the union and its member states are among the main actors in the protection and implementation of women's rights, which they also defend in their external relations. the year 2015 is an important year as it marks both the adoption of the post-2015 development agenda, the 15th anniversary of un security council resolution 1325 on women, peace and security, and the 20th anniversary of the adoption of the beijing declaration and programme of action. it is in this context that the union and its member states are continuing and intensifying their efforts in a matter which they regard as a priority. during the second half of the year, the luxembourg presidency will continue the work carried out in recent years in the council on gender and development. it is based in particular on the conclusions adopted by the council last may on gender equality in development. the presidency will ensure that gender issues remain at the heart of the priorities of the union and its member states, both within the union and in its external policy. within the council bodies, we are currently working with the member states, the commission and the european external action service on the implementation of the new action plan for gender equality and women's empowerment. globally, significant progress has been made in gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. access to primary education for girls has improved significantly in recent years. women's economic empowerment is progressing. more women now have access to health care and modern contraceptive methods, and maternal mortality has decreased considerably. however, it must be admitted that progress is not as rapid as we would like and that it is very unevenly spread between regions, between countries and sometimes even within the same country. every day, around the world, the rights of women and girls continue to be violated: access to education is denied, discrimination in employment, lower pay for equal work, discriminatory or harassing laws, domestic violence, trafficking and sexual exploitation, and female genital mutilation. all these examples remind us of the need for the european union not to slacken its efforts, but to intensify them decisively. we want the new action plan recently presented by the commission to be an effective tool for promoting the rights of women and girls. it must make it possible to significantly improve the situation of women and girls, who are still the victims of discrimination. we welcome the fact that reports on the implementation of the new action plan are mandatory and are planned as a joint exercise between the various actors in the european union. another innovative approach is the institutional cultural shift envisaged by the document which calls on eu delegations, both at headquarters and in the field, to integrate gender in an automatic and transversal way in all sectors. in the coming days and weeks we will continue to work actively in the council on this matter. a gender and development item will be on the agenda of the foreign affairs council meeting with the development ministers on 26 october. the council will adopt conclusions and the new action plan for equality between men and women. ladies and gentlemen, the european union and the member states must remain at the forefront of the fight for equality between men and women. the presidency will make every effort to do so.
